c-us7-ov-gdp.text: In the Bureau of Economic Analysis's series, in billions of chained 2017 dollars, real GDP was 2,500.1 in 1945, 2,458.5 in 1950, 3,083.0 in 1955, 3,500.3 in 1960, 4,478.6 in 1965, 5,316.4 in 1970, 6,060.9 in 1975 and 7,257.3 in 1980. From 1950 to 1980 it roughly tripled.
c-us7-ov-gdp.label: approx
c-us7-ov-gdp.note: Chained-dollar levels change with each BEA revision. 'Roughly tripled' is this book's arithmetic: 7,257.3 is about 2.95 times 2,458.5.

c-us7-ov-pop.text: In BEA's series, in thousands, the population was 139,928 in 1945, 151,684 in 1950, 165,275 in 1955, 180,760 in 1960, 194,347 in 1965, 205,089 in 1970, 215,981 in 1975 and 227,726 in 1980: from about 140 million to about 228 million.
c-us7-ov-pop.label: consensus

c-us7-ov-percap.text: Dividing BEA's real GDP by its population, real GDP per person was about $16,200 in 1950 and about $31,900 in 1980, in chained 2017 dollars: roughly double. Population grew by about half over the same years.
c-us7-ov-percap.label: approx
c-us7-ov-percap.note: This book's arithmetic from two BEA series, rounded to the nearest hundred dollars.

c-us7-ov-income.text: In the Census Bureau's series, in 2025 C-CPI-U dollars, real median family income was 41,880 in 1953 (the series' first year), 43,380 in 1955, 49,960 in 1960, 58,090 in 1965, 68,340 in 1970, 73,000 in 1973, 69,850 in 1975 and 73,230 in 1980: a rise of about 74 percent from 1953 to 1973, then little change to 1980.
c-us7-ov-income.label: approx
c-us7-ov-income.note: The series is now expressed in C-CPI-U dollars (R-CPI-U-RS before 2000), a changed deflator, so its dollar levels differ from older printed tables. It begins in 1953. The percentage is this book's arithmetic.

c-us7-ov-poverty.text: The official poverty rate, in the Census Bureau's series, was 22.4 percent in 1959, the first year measured; 22.2 in 1960, 17.3 in 1965, 12.6 in 1970, 11.1 in 1973, 12.3 in 1975 and 13.0 in 1980.
c-us7-ov-poverty.label: consensus

c-us7-cont-telegram.text: On 22 February 1946 George Kennan, the American chargé d'affaires in the Soviet Union, sent the Secretary of State the message known as the Long Telegram.
c-us7-cont-telegram.label: consensus

c-us7-cont-kennan.text: In the Long Telegram Kennan described Soviet power as 'a political force committed fanatically to the belief that with US there can be no permanent modus vivendi', and as 'Impervious to logic of reason, and it is highly sensitive to logic of force.'
c-us7-cont-kennan.label: consensus

c-us7-cont-x.text: Kennan's views also appeared in what the Office of the Historian calls 'an anonymous contribution to the journal Foreign Affairs, the so-called "X-Article."'
c-us7-cont-x.label: consensus

c-us7-cont-truman.text: The Truman Doctrine of 12 March 1947 declared: 'I believe that it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures.' Truman requested $400,000,000 for Greece and Turkey.
c-us7-cont-truman.label: consensus

c-us7-cont-marshall.text: George Marshall announced the plan that bears his name in a speech to the graduating class at Harvard University on 5 June 1947, and Congress approved funding that would eventually rise to over $12 billion.
c-us7-cont-marshall.label: approx
c-us7-cont-marshall.note: The Office of the Historian's round figure; this book has no breakdown by country or year.

c-us7-cont-berlin.text: The Berlin crisis, a Soviet blockade of West Berlin, began on 24 June 1948. In the American airlift that answered it, 'one plane landed every 45 seconds at Tempelhof Airport'. The blockade ended on 12 May 1949.
c-us7-cont-berlin.label: approx
c-us7-cont-berlin.note: The same Office of the Historian page gives both 12 May and 11 May 1949 for the end.

c-us7-cont-nato.text: The North Atlantic Treaty was signed in Washington on 4 April 1949. Its members 'agreed to consider attack against one an attack against all.'
c-us7-cont-nato.label: consensus

c-us7-cont-nsc68.text: NSC-68 was 'completed by the U.S. Department of State's Policy Planning Staff on April 7, 1950' and called for a massive build-up. After the Korean War began, defense spending 'almost tripled', rising from 5 to 14.2 percent of GDP between 1950 and 1953.
c-us7-cont-nsc68.label: consensus

c-us7-cont-orthodox.text: The orthodox historians of the Cold War, in Seth Center's summary, 'place primary responsibility for the Cold War on the Soviet Union'; many of them were 'former Roosevelt or Truman administration officials'. Center names Herbert Feis, among whose books is From Trust to Terror: The Onset of the Cold War, 1945-1950, and writes that these works 'emphasize Stalin's "ruthlessness," "spirit of mistrust," and revolutionary goals.'
c-us7-cont-orthodox.label: debated
c-us7-cont-orthodox.note: Given in Seth Center's summary, not in Feis's own words; the inner quotation marks around 'ruthlessness' and 'spirit of mistrust' are Center's. Revisionists, also on this page, stressed American ambitions instead.

c-us7-cont-revisionist.text: Revisionist historians, among them William Appleman Williams in The Tragedy of American Diplomacy (1959), argued, as Verso's online encyclopedia summarises them, that the United States had long had imperial ambitions.
c-us7-cont-revisionist.label: debated
c-us7-cont-revisionist.note: Given here only as a secondary summary, not in Williams's own words. Against it stand the orthodox school, as Seth Center summarises it, and the later view of Gaddis, set out on this page through Center's summary and Ascherson's review of We Now Know.

c-us7-cont-gaddis.text: In 1983 John Lewis Gaddis described 'The Emerging Post-Revisionist Synthesis on the Origins of the Cold War'. Seth Center calls Gaddis that synthesis's 'first and foremost proponent' and writes that he 'concludes that the conflict grew out of external and internal conflict in both the Soviet Union and the United States.'
c-us7-cont-gaddis.label: debated
c-us7-cont-gaddis.note: The 1983 article is cited by title only; Gaddis's view is given in Center's words, not in his own, and Center does not refer to the 1983 article. It names a position between the revisionists and the orthodox school.

c-us7-cont-archives.text: For We Now Know (1997), Gaddis drew on newly opened Soviet archives. Reviewing it, Neal Ascherson described Gaddis as convinced that Stalin, more than anyone or anything else, brought about the Cold War, and wrote that the archives settled that Kim Il Sung had attacked South Korea first, in 1950.
c-us7-cont-archives.label: debated
c-us7-cont-archives.note: Gaddis's view is given as his reviewer, Ascherson, summarised it, not in Gaddis's own words. Revisionists, as summarised on this page, stressed American ambitions instead.

c-us7-red-loyalty.text: Executive Order 9835, of 21 March 1947, provided: 'There shall be a loyalty investigation of every person entering the civilian employment of any department or agency' of the federal executive.
c-us7-red-loyalty.label: consensus

c-us7-red-hollywood.text: In October 1947 the Hollywood Ten refused to answer the questions of the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC), sitting in Washington. They were 'voted in contempt of Congress on November 24, 1947', received 'sentences of six months to one year in prison', and were blacklisted.
c-us7-red-hollywood.label: consensus

c-us7-red-hiss.text: Whittaker Chambers accused Alger Hiss in 1948. On 21 January 1950 Hiss was found 'Guilty on two counts of perjury' and was sentenced to five years.
c-us7-red-hiss.label: consensus

c-us7-red-rosenberg.text: In the case the FBI calls the atom spy case, 'On March 29, 1951, the jury rendered a verdict of guilty' against Julius and Ethel Rosenberg. Both were executed on 19 June 1953: 'At 8:05 p.m. on June 19, 1953, Julius Rosenberg was executed'.
c-us7-red-rosenberg.label: consensus

c-us7-red-venona.text: The United States 'began a secret program in February 1943 later codenamed VENONA' to break Soviet cables. It ran until 1980. 'The first of six public releases of translated VENONA messages was made in July 1995' and 'included 49 messages'; 'Over the course of five more releases, all of the approximately 3,000 VENONA translations were made public.'
c-us7-red-venona.label: consensus

c-us7-red-osti.text: The Department of Energy's history of the Manhattan Project names 'Julius Rosenberg, and Rosenberg's wife Ethel' among the spies Venona uncovered.
c-us7-red-osti.label: consensus

c-us7-red-ethel.text: Ethel Rosenberg's own part is disputed. A memo of 22 August 1950 by the codebreaker Meredith Gardner, which the Associated Press described in 2024 as recently declassified, concluded that she knew of her husband's work 'but that due to illness she did not engage in the work herself'. The historian Harvey Klehr, as the AP reports, has written that she 'was an active participant in her husband's spy network.'
c-us7-red-ethel.label: debated
c-us7-red-ethel.note: Two readings of the evidence, both as the Associated Press reports them: Gardner's memo, which her sons obtained, against Klehr's view that she took an active part.

c-us7-red-wheeling.text: At Wheeling, West Virginia, on 9 February 1950, Senator Joseph McCarthy said, in the text printed by History Matters: 'I have here in my hand a list of 205 . . . a list of names that were made known to the Secretary of State'. The number is disputed: History Matters notes that advance copies of the speech given to the press 'record the number as 205', but that in a letter to President Truman the next day and in the transcript McCarthy submitted to the Congressional Record ten days later 'he uses the number 57.'
c-us7-red-wheeling.label: approx
c-us7-red-wheeling.note: The number McCarthy gave at Wheeling is disputed; History Matters gives 205 from the advance press copies and 57 from his later letter and transcript.

c-us7-red-censure.text: The televised Army-McCarthy hearings, which began on 22 April 1954, 'showed McCarthy in an increasingly unattractive light'. On 2 December 1954 the Senate, 'on a vote of 67 to 22, censured Joseph McCarthy.'
c-us7-red-censure.label: consensus

c-us7-red-haynes.text: Haynes and Klehr, authors of Venona (Yale University Press) and In Denial (2003), argue that Soviet espionage was extensive. Encounter Books' description of In Denial says the book charges revisionist scholars with ignoring or distorting new evidence from recently opened Russian archives.
c-us7-red-haynes.label: debated
c-us7-red-haynes.note: Their case is given here only as their publisher describes it, not in their own words. Schrecker, also on this page, stresses instead the harm the anticommunist crusade did.

c-us7-red-schrecker.text: The publisher's description of Ellen Schrecker's Many Are the Crimes (1998), reproduced by the National Humanities Center, calls it 'the first post-Cold War exploration of the anticommunist witch-hunt and its devastating impact'. Reviewing it, Alan Wald quotes her asking whether 'the espionage, which unquestionably occurred' required 'a politically repressive internal security system', and reports that her answer is no.
c-us7-red-schrecker.label: debated
c-us7-red-schrecker.note: Her case is given through her publisher's description of the book and a review that quotes her; her own words appear only as Wald quotes them. Haynes and Klehr, also on this page, stress the extent of Soviet espionage.

c-us7-kor-deaths.text: The Department of Veterans Affairs counts 33,739 American battle deaths in the Korean War and 2,835 other deaths in theater, 36,574 in all; the same fact sheet lists 17,672 'Other Deaths in Service (Non-Theater)'. The three figures together come to 54,246. The National Park Service writes of 'over 50,000 American deaths'. The historian Allan R. Millett explains that the Defense Department's older figures for 'other deaths' appear to have 'included all noncombat deaths throughout the armed forces, worldwide, during the entire Korean War era (1950–57)'.
c-us7-kor-deaths.label: approx
c-us7-kor-deaths.note: The gap is a matter of what is counted: 36,574 is the VA's count for the Korean theater, while the NPS's round 'over 50,000' matches the VA's three lines combined, 54,246 (this book's sum), which include deaths in service outside the theater. Millett traces the larger figure to the counting of noncombat deaths worldwide.

c-us7-kor-macarthur.text: 'On April 11, 1951, President Truman officially relieved Douglas MacArthur of his command'. As the Truman Library puts Truman's reasoning, he felt the general had 'overstepped his authority, defied direct orders from his superior'.
c-us7-kor-macarthur.label: consensus

c-us7-kor-armistice.text: In 1952 Eisenhower pledged that 'he would personally go to Korea'. Armistice negotiations had gone on at Panmunjom, North Korea, for two years when, 'Finally, on July 27, 1953', the armistice was signed.
c-us7-kor-armistice.label: consensus

c-us7-kor-highway.text: The Federal-Aid Highway Act, signed on 29 June 1956, 'increases the Interstate System to 41,000 miles' (from 40,000 miles authorized in 1944) and paid for it. It 'authorizes $25 billion over the period 1957-1969 as the Federal share (90 percent)' and 'establishes the Highway Trust Fund.' The Senate's history of the act ties the roads to defense: 'transporting troops and for evacuating cities in case of nuclear attack'.
c-us7-kor-highway.label: consensus

c-us7-kor-sputnik.text: Of Sputnik's launch on 4 October 1957 the Office of the Historian writes: 'The successful launch came as a shock to experts and citizens in the United States'. Congress answered with the National Defense Education Act, which 'made substantial funds available for low-cost student loans' and supported science, mathematics and foreign languages.
c-us7-kor-sputnik.label: consensus

c-us7-kor-farewell.text: In his farewell address of 17 January 1961 Eisenhower said: 'In the councils of government, we must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence, whether sought or unsought, by the military-industrial complex. The potential for the disastrous rise of misplaced power exists and will persist.' He also warned that public policy 'could itself become the captive of a scientific-technological elite.'
c-us7-kor-farewell.label: consensus

c-us7-boom-gibill.text: The GI Bill was signed on 22 June 1944. By 1956 '7.8 million of 16 million World War II veterans had participated in an education or training program', and from 1944 to 1952 the 'VA backed nearly 2.4 million home loans'.
c-us7-boom-gibill.label: consensus

c-us7-boom-katznelson.text: As Publishers Weekly's review summarises Katznelson's When Affirmative Action Was White (2005), the bill unfairly favoured white veterans by turning the administration of benefits over to local governments.
c-us7-boom-katznelson.label: debated
c-us7-boom-katznelson.note: Katznelson's case is given here only in a reviewer's summary, not in his own words. Turner and Bound, Mettler, Agbai, and Althoff and Szerman, all on this page, find broader gains, mixed effects or widening gaps.

c-us7-boom-turner.text: Turner and Bound (2002) find in their abstract 'a substantial and positive impact on the educational attainment of white men and black men born outside the South', but that 'for those black veterans likely to be limited to the South in their educational choices, the G.I. Bill had little effect on collegiate outcomes', 'resulting in the exacerbation of the educational differences between black and white men from southern states.'
c-us7-boom-turner.label: debated
c-us7-boom-turner.note: A mixed finding from an NBER working paper (2002): gains for white men and for Black men born outside the South, little effect for Black veterans likely limited to the South in their educational choices.

c-us7-boom-mettler.text: The description of Mettler's Soldiers to Citizens by her literary agency presents the bill's benefits as reaching across lines of class and race.
c-us7-boom-mettler.label: debated
c-us7-boom-mettler.note: Given only as the agency's description of the book, not in Mettler's own words. Katznelson, Agbai, and Althoff and Szerman stress racial inequality instead.

c-us7-boom-new.text: Agbai, in the American Journal of Sociology (2025), studies the bill's home-loan guaranty. Her abstract finds that 'the GI Bill is linked with increased homeownership and home value for Black and White veterans', but that 'the policy exacerbated extant racial inequalities'. Althoff and Szerman, in a working paper of June 2026, estimate 'a 5-percentage-point (47 percent) widening of the racial college gap'.
c-us7-boom-new.label: debated
c-us7-boom-new.note: New findings. Agbai's is a peer-reviewed article on housing, not college; Althoff and Szerman's CEP discussion paper has not yet been peer reviewed. Mettler and Turner and Bound, on this page, find broad or regional gains.

c-us7-boom-levittown.text: Levittown, on Long Island, begun in 1947, barred Black families. Its Clause 25 read: 'No dwelling shall be used or occupied by members of other than the Caucasian race'. It had 17,447 homes by November 1951. In the Searchable Museum's words, 'Levittown refused to house Black veterans and their families.'
c-us7-boom-levittown.label: consensus

c-us7-boom-births.text: Pew Research Center, from NCHS data, counts 'a total of 76 million births during the boom' of 1946-1964, with annual births 'surpassing 4 million in 1954 and remaining above that level until 1965.'
c-us7-boom-births.label: approx
c-us7-boom-births.note: A round total from Pew's reading of NCHS birth data.

c-us7-boom-unions.text: Union membership peaked at about a third of workers. The Congressional Research Service cites 'a peak of 34.2% in 1945' in one series and 'its post-World War II peak of 33.5% in 1954' in another. In 2022, '10.1% of all employed wage and salary workers were members of unions'; on the measure behind the 1945 peak, union members as a share of total nonfarm employment, the 2022 figure was 9.4 percent.
c-us7-boom-unions.label: approx
c-us7-boom-unions.note: The peak year and level depend on the series used; figures before 1983 were compiled by Richard Freeman. The 2022 figures are 10.1 percent (BLS, wage and salary workers) and 9.4 percent (CRS, over total nonfarm employment).

c-us7-boom-pledge.text: 'Under God' entered the Pledge of Allegiance on 14 June 1954. Signing the bill, Eisenhower said that 'the millions of our school children will daily proclaim ... the dedication of our nation and our people to the Almighty.'
c-us7-boom-pledge.label: consensus

c-us7-boom-motto.text: 'In God we trust' became the national motto under a law 'approved by the President on July 30, 1956' (Public Law 84-851), and was 'first used on paper money in 1957'.
c-us7-boom-motto.label: consensus

c-us7-boom-church.text: Gallup found church membership at 73 percent in 1937; it 'remained near 70% for the next six decades', and in 2020 '47% of Americans said they belonged to a church, synagogue or mosque'.
c-us7-boom-church.label: approx
c-us7-boom-church.note: Gallup's page gives no year-by-year figures for 1945-1980, only that membership stayed near 70 percent.

c-us7-cr1-eo9981.text: On 26 July 1948 President Truman issued Executive Order 9981, which declared 'equality of treatment and opportunity for all persons in the armed services'. The National Archives states that 'by the end of the Korean conflict, almost all of the military was integrated.'
c-us7-cr1-eo9981.label: consensus

c-us7-cr1-manifesto.text: On 12 March 1956 the Southern Manifesto, signed by 82 representatives and 19 senators, all from former Confederate states, was introduced in the House. In the House historians' words, it 'attacked Brown as an abuse of judicial power that trespassed upon states' rights' and urged southerners to exhaust all 'lawful means' of resistance to school desegregation.
c-us7-cr1-manifesto.label: consensus

c-us7-cr1-till.text: Emmett Till, a 14-year-old visiting relatives in Mississippi, was 'lynched on Aug. 28, 1955.' At the Tallahatchie County Second District Courthouse in Sumner, 'An all-white, all-male jury was selected and ultimately acquitted Roy Bryant and J.W. Milam', who 'later confessed to their crimes in a paid interview.'
c-us7-cr1-till.label: consensus

c-us7-cr1-monument.text: On 25 July 2023 President Biden established the Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley National Monument, which the National Park Service calls America's 425th national park, at three sites: Graball Landing near Glendora, Mississippi, 'believed to be the site where Till's brutalized body was recovered from the Tallahatchie River'; Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ in Chicago, 'the site of Till's widely attended open casket visitation and funeral'; and the courthouse in Sumner.
c-us7-cr1-monument.label: consensus

c-us7-cr1-antilynch.text: The Emmett Till Antilynching Act became law on 29 March 2022 and 'sets a maximum sentence of 30 years in prison.' The House had passed it 422 to 3 ('The yeas are 422. The nays are 3'). PBS NewsHour reports that Congress had failed to act against lynching 'more than 200 times' since 1900.
c-us7-cr1-antilynch.label: consensus

c-us7-cr1-boycott.text: Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery on 1 December 1955. The bus boycott ran from 5 December 1955 to 20 December 1956; the new Montgomery Improvement Association elected Martin Luther King Jr. its president. In Browder v. Gayle, 'bus segregation was unconstitutional', and the Supreme Court affirmed the ruling in November 1956.
c-us7-cr1-boycott.label: consensus

c-us7-cr1-littlerock.text: On 17 May 1954 the Supreme Court ruled in Brown v. Board of Education that segregated schools were 'inherently unequal.' In September 1957 Governor Faubus of Arkansas called out 'the state's National Guard to surround Little Rock Central High School'; on 4 September the nine Black students known as the Little Rock Nine attempted to enter. Eisenhower's Executive Order 10730, which the National Archives dates 23 September 1957 (its transcript is signed 24 September), placed the Arkansas National Guard under federal control and 'sent 1,000 U.S. Army paratroopers from the 101st Airborne Division'.
c-us7-cr1-littlerock.label: consensus

c-us7-cr1-sclc.text: The Southern Christian Leadership Conference, founded in January 1957 at Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta, 'drew on the power and independence of black churches' in its aim to redeem 'the soul of America.'
c-us7-cr1-sclc.label: consensus

c-us7-cr1-bu.text: At Boston University King studied personalism, in the King Institute's words 'a philosophy that emphasizes the necessity of personal religious experience in understanding God', under Brightman and DeWolf, and received his PhD in June 1955.
c-us7-cr1-bu.label: consensus

c-us7-cr1-king.text: In 'Pilgrimage to Nonviolence' (1960) King wrote that Rauschenbusch's Christianity and the Social Crisis was a book that 'left an indelible imprint on my thinking', that 'Christ furnished the spirit and motivation while Gandhi furnished the method', and that Niebuhr 'made me aware of the complexity of human motives.'
c-us7-cr1-king.label: consensus

c-us7-cr2-sitins.text: On 1 February 1960 four students from North Carolina A&T sat in at the Woolworth's store in Greensboro. 'By the end of April over 50,000 students had participated', and the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) was founded on 15-17 April 1960.
c-us7-cr2-sitins.label: approx
c-us7-cr2-sitins.note: The number of participants is the King Institute's round figure.

c-us7-cr2-rides.text: The Freedom Riders left Washington on 4 May 1961. Near Anniston, Alabama, 'one of the buses was firebombed', and in Birmingham 'Bull' Connor's police 'offered no protection.' The Interstate Commerce Commission's ban on segregation took effect on '1 November 1961.'
c-us7-cr2-rides.label: consensus

c-us7-cr2-bham.text: The Birmingham campaign began on 3 April 1963. King was arrested on 12 April, Good Friday. On 3 May 'Commissioner Connor directed local police and fire departments to use force', and on 15 September Klansmen bombed the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church, 'killing four young girls.'
c-us7-cr2-bham.label: consensus

c-us7-cr2-letter.text: King dated his Letter from Birmingham Jail 16 April 1963. In it he wrote: 'Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.' He wrote: 'This "Wait" has almost always meant "Never."' He asked: 'Was not Amos an extremist for justice: "Let justice roll down like waters and righteousness like an ever flowing stream."' and next: 'Was not Paul an extremist for the Christian gospel: "I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus."'
c-us7-cr2-letter.label: consensus

c-us7-cr2-amos.text: The Revised Standard Version renders Amos 5:24: 'But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an everflowing stream.' The NRSVUE renders it: 'But let justice roll down like water and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.'
c-us7-cr2-amos.label: consensus

c-us7-cr2-march.text: The March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom on 28 August 1963, with Bayard Rustin as 'march organizer', drew 'more than 200,000 demonstrators.' A. Philip Randolph had first called for a march on Washington in 1941, and on 26 March 1963 he telegraphed King that the Negro American Labor Council had begun planning a June march 'for Negro job rights'.
c-us7-cr2-march.label: approx
c-us7-cr2-march.note: A crowd estimate, given by the King Institute as a lower bound.

c-us7-cr2-house.text: The House of Representatives passed the civil rights bill on 10 February 1964, '290 to 130.'
c-us7-cr2-house.label: consensus

c-us7-cr2-party.text: By party and region, the House vote of 10 February 1964 was: Democrats 152 to 96 (Northern Democrats 141 to 4, Southern Democrats 11 to 92) and Republicans 138 to 34.
c-us7-cr2-party.label: approx
c-us7-cr2-party.note: From a 1964 congressional report reproduced by the Civil Rights Movement Archive, whose publisher is not stated on the copy. The party figures add up to the official total of 290 to 130 recorded by the National Archives.

c-us7-cr2-senate.text: The Senate 'debated the bill for sixty days, including seven Saturdays.' On 10 June 1964 it 'voted 71 to 29 for cloture', with a coalition of 27 Republicans and 44 Democrats; it passed the bill nine days later, and Johnson signed it on 2 July 1964.
c-us7-cr2-senate.label: consensus

c-us7-cr2-fs.text: In the Freedom Summer of 1964, Michael Schwerner, James Chaney and Andrew Goodman disappeared in Mississippi on 21 June. Their bodies were found on 4 August '14 feet below an earthen dam.' In 1967 seven men were convicted, 'none on murder charges', and Edgar Ray Killen was 'convicted of manslaughter on June 21, 2005.'
c-us7-cr2-fs.label: consensus

c-us7-cr2-mfdp.text: At the 1964 Democratic convention Fannie Lou Hamer of the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party told the credentials committee: 'If the Freedom Democratic Party is not seated now, I question America.' Offered a compromise of two at-large seats, Hamer replied: 'We didn't come all this way for no two seats.'
c-us7-cr2-mfdp.label: consensus

c-us7-cr2-selma.text: Jimmie Lee Jackson was shot on 18 February 1965. 'Bloody Sunday' at the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma followed on 7 March. The march ran from 'March 21, 1965 to March 25, 1965' and swelled to 25,000 at Montgomery. Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act on 6 August 1965.
c-us7-cr2-selma.label: approx
c-us7-cr2-selma.note: The figure of 25,000 is a crowd estimate. A footnote on the King Institute page misdates the signing of the Act to 1966; its main text gives 1965.

c-us7-cr2-reg.text: Black voter registration in seven southern states, percent, March 1965 and November 1988 (white registration in brackets): Alabama 19.3 (69.2) and 68.4 (75.0); Georgia 27.4 (62.6) and 56.8 (63.9); Louisiana 31.6 (80.5) and 77.1 (75.1); Mississippi 6.7 (69.9) and 74.2 (80.5); North Carolina 46.8 (96.8) and 58.2 (65.6); South Carolina 37.3 (75.7) and 56.7 (61.8); Virginia 38.3 (61.1) and 63.8 (68.5).
c-us7-cr2-reg.label: approx
c-us7-cr2-reg.note: As printed in the Justice Department's table, adapted from Grofman, Handley and Niemi (1992). North Carolina's white rate for 1965, 96.8 percent, is given as printed, though it is far above the other states' rates.

c-us7-gs-cuba.text: A U-2 flight on 14 October 1962 photographed missile sites in Cuba. Kennedy announced a 'quarantine' on 22 October, and on 28 October Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles. The United States pledged not to invade Cuba. Robert Kennedy told the Soviet ambassador, Anatoly Dobrynin, that the United States planned to remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey soon, but 'this could not be part of any public resolution of the missile crisis'; 'U.S. Jupiter missiles were removed from Turkey in April 1963.'
c-us7-gs-cuba.label: consensus

c-us7-gs-jfk.text: President Kennedy was killed in Dealey Plaza, Dallas, on 22 November 1963. The Warren Commission concluded that 'Oswald acted alone.'
c-us7-gs-jfk.label: consensus

c-us7-gs-files.text: Under Executive Order 14176 the National Archives released JFK assassination records in batches: 31,419 pages and 37,127 pages on 18 March 2025, 14,318 pages on 20 March, 53 pages on 26 March and 704 pages on 3 April 2025, and '11,022 pages' on 30 January 2026.
c-us7-gs-files.label: consensus

c-us7-gs-wop.text: In his State of the Union message of 8 January 1964 Johnson said: 'This administration today, here and now, declares unconditional war on poverty in America.'
c-us7-gs-wop.label: consensus

c-us7-gs-aged.text: The poverty rate of the aged fell from 35.2 percent in 1959 to 16.3 percent in 1973.
c-us7-gs-aged.label: consensus

c-us7-gs-medicare.text: On 30 July 1965, at the Truman Library in Independence, Missouri, Johnson signed the 'Social Security Amendments of 1965', which created Medicare and, under Title XIX, Medicaid. Harry and Bess Truman 'received the first Medicare insurance cards.'
c-us7-gs-medicare.label: consensus

c-us7-gs-hc.text: On 3 October 1965, on Liberty Island, Johnson signed the immigration bill known as Hart-Celler, saying: 'This bill that we will sign today is not a revolutionary bill.' He condemned 'the harsh injustice of the national origins quota system'. The Act 'abolished this quota system' and set caps of 120,000 for the Western Hemisphere and 170,000 for the rest of the world.
c-us7-gs-hc.label: consensus

c-us7-gs-pew.text: Pew Research Center (2015) estimates that 'roughly 59 million immigrants' came to the United States from 1965 to 2015, that the foreign-born share of the population rose 'from 5% in 1965 to 14%', and that of these immigrants 'half (51%) are from Latin America and one-quarter are from Asia.'
c-us7-gs-pew.label: approx
c-us7-gs-pew.note: Pew's estimates, rounded; the 14 percent share is for 2015.

c-us7-gs-murray.text: Charles Murray's Losing Ground (1984), as the Manhattan Institute describes it, argues that the ambitious social programmes of the 1960s and 1970s actually made matters worse for their supposed beneficiaries, the poor and minorities.
c-us7-gs-murray.label: debated
c-us7-gs-murray.note: The critics' case, given in the Institute's summary, not Murray's words. Bailey and Danziger, Wimer and his co-authors, and Burkhauser and his co-authors all find that poverty fell, by different measures.

c-us7-gs-legacies.text: The contributors to Legacies of the War on Poverty (2013), edited by Martha J. Bailey and Sheldon Danziger, judge, as their publisher summarises the book, that the popular view that the War on Poverty failed is too negative.
c-us7-gs-legacies.label: debated
c-us7-gs-legacies.note: The defenders' case, given in the publisher's summary. Murray, as the Manhattan Institute describes his book, argues the opposite.

c-us7-gs-wimer.text: Christopher Wimer and his co-authors (2016), using an anchored Supplemental Poverty Measure, find that from 1967 to 2012 'poverty rates have dropped by 40 %' and that 'government policies, not market incomes, are driving the declines.'
c-us7-gs-wimer.label: debated
c-us7-gs-wimer.note: From the paper's own abstract. Murray, as the Manhattan Institute describes his book, argues that the programmes harmed their beneficiaries; Burkhauser and his co-authors, on a full-income measure, find a larger fall.

c-us7-gs-burk.text: Richard Burkhauser, Kevin Corinth, James Elwell and Jeff Larrimore, using an absolute Full-income Poverty Measure (FPM), report that 'our absolute FPM rate fell from 19.5 to 1.6 percent' from 1963 to 2019, which 'reflects increases in full income throughout the distribution', but that 'reductions in relative poverty since 1963 have been far more modest, falling from 19.5 to 16.0 percent in 2019.'
c-us7-gs-burk.label: debated
c-us7-gs-burk.note: From the NBER abstract. On an absolute measure the war on poverty was largely won; on a relative measure it was not. Others, such as Wimer and his co-authors, use an anchored measure and reach a smaller decline.

c-us7-viet-tonkin.text: The Tonkin Gulf Resolution, passed on 7 August 1964, approved the president's determination 'to take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack against the forces of the United States'. A National Security Agency report of 2002, made available in 2007, confirmed the attack of 2 August and 'concluded the August 4 attack never happened.' 'The Resolution was repealed in January 1971 in an attempt to curtail President Nixon's power to continue the war.'
c-us7-viet-tonkin.label: consensus

c-us7-viet-votes.text: The Senate passed the resolution 88 to 2, with Senators Morse and Gruening against. The State Department's documentary history records that it 'passed the Senate (88–2) and the House of Representatives (416–0) on August 7', and the Voteview roll-call record gives the House vote as 416-0, as does James M. Lindsay of the Council on Foreign Relations. Britannica and the Defense Department's Vietnam War commemoration give 414 to 0.
c-us7-viet-votes.label: approx
c-us7-viet-votes.note: The State Department's documentary history and the roll-call record give 416-0; Britannica and the Defense Department's commemoration give 414-0. All agree that no member of the House voted against.

c-us7-viet-troops.text: U.S. military personnel in Vietnam at the end of each year or half-year, by Edwin Moïse's tabulation: 1964 23,300; 1965 184,000; 1966 385,000; 1967 486,000; 1968 537,000; 1969 539,000 (end of first half) and 474,000 (end of year); 1970 336,000; 1971 158,000; 1972 24,000.
c-us7-viet-troops.label: approx
c-us7-viet-troops.note: Rounded figures from a historian's table that cites no source.

c-us7-viet-deaths.text: The National Archives lists 58,220 U.S. military fatal casualties in the war, 47,434 hostile and 10,786 non-hostile. By year: 1964 216; 1965 1,928; 1966 6,350; 1967 11,363; 1968 16,899; 1969 11,780; 1970 6,173; 1971 2,414; 1972 759; 1973 68.
c-us7-viet-deaths.label: approx
c-us7-viet-deaths.note: The Archives calls the counts informational, with data 'current as of April 29, 2008'.

c-us7-viet-tet.text: The Tet offensive began on 30 January 1968, when about 84,000 troops attacked 36 provincial capitals and 64 district towns. In the Defense Department commemoration's words, 'The offensive shocks the American public.'
c-us7-viet-tet.label: approx
c-us7-viet-tet.note: The number of attacking troops is an estimate.

c-us7-viet-draft.text: 'A lottery drawing – the first since 1942 – was held on December 1, 1969', for men born from 1944 to 1950; the first date drawn was 'September 14.' The last draft call was issued on 7 December 1972, and the authority to induct ended on 30 June 1973.
c-us7-viet-draft.label: consensus

c-us7-viet-mora.text: On 15 October 1969, 'Over two million people across the United States' took part in the Moratorium to End the War in Vietnam.
c-us7-viet-mora.label: approx
c-us7-viet-mora.note: A round estimate of participants across the country.

c-us7-viet-kent.text: At Kent State University on 4 May 1970 the Ohio National Guard fired 'between 61 and 67 shots' in 'a 13-second period', 'killing four and wounding nine.'
c-us7-viet-kent.label: approx
c-us7-viet-kent.note: The university gives the number of shots as a range.

c-us7-viet-jackson.text: At Jackson State on 14-15 May 1970, city police and highway patrolmen fired 'nearly 400 rounds of bullets and buckshot over 28 seconds in every direction'; they 'turned on Alexander Hall, a women's dormitory.' Phillip Gibbs and James Green were killed, and 'Twelve people were shot by the police and survived.'
c-us7-viet-jackson.label: approx
c-us7-viet-jackson.note: The number of rounds is an estimate.

c-us7-viet-pp.text: The Pentagon Papers, the 'Report of the Office of the Secretary of Defense Vietnam Task Force', commissioned by McNamara in 1967 and about 7,000 pages long, were leaked in June 1971 and released in full in 2011. In New York Times Co. v. United States (30 June 1971) the Court stated: 'Any system of prior restraints of expression comes to this Court bearing a heavy presumption against its constitutional validity.'
c-us7-viet-pp.label: consensus

c-us7-viet-saigon.text: The peace agreement was signed on 27 January 1973. Operation Frequent Wind, on 29 April 1975, took 'over 7,000 personnel—primarily Americans and Vietnamese' out of Saigon. 'On April 30, 1975, NVA tanks rolled through the gate of the Presidential Palace in Saigon, effectively ending the war.'
c-us7-viet-saigon.label: consensus

c-us7-viet-kort.text: The historian Michael G. Kort, who himself argues that the war 'could and should have been won at far less cost than the United States, South Vietnam, and their allies suffered in defeat', frames the debate as two questions: whether the war was necessary and wise, that is, vital to American security interests, and, once the United States was involved, 'was that war winnable?' The orthodox narrative, whose 'articulate proponents' he says include the journalists David Halberstam, Frances FitzGerald, Stanley Karnow and Neil Sheehan, and which he says 'also became the prevailing viewpoint among American academics', 'answers both questions firmly in the negative.' The revisionist narrative answers both in the affirmative, holding that the United States went to war 'without first developing a strategy for victory'.
c-us7-viet-kort.label: debated
c-us7-viet-kort.note: Kort's own summary of the two schools; Kort himself is on the revisionist side, as his own blog post on the book states. He cites Andrew Wiest on how the view that the war had been a mistake and a tragedy became accepted wisdom.

c-us7-viet-logevall.text: Fredrik Logevall, author of Choosing War (1999), said: 'The Vietnam tragedy, which we are still living with in so many ways, which led to deaths of millions, was an unnecessary war'.
c-us7-viet-logevall.label: debated
c-us7-viet-logevall.note: Logevall's own words, as quoted in his university's news release of 1999. Revisionists such as Moyar, also on this page, argue against this view.

c-us7-viet-moyar.text: Mark Moyar's Triumph Forsaken (2006), which James McAllister, as Moyar quotes him, said 'can rightfully claim to be the most consequential revisionist book ever produced on the Vietnam War', shows, in Moyar's own description, 'how Diem consolidated control over a badly fractured country and defeated the underground Communists' in its early chapters, and in its later ones 'how the removal of Diem crippled South Vietnam's ability to fight the Communists.'
c-us7-viet-moyar.label: debated
c-us7-viet-moyar.note: The revisionist case, from Moyar's response in an H-Diplo roundtable (2007). Chapman and Gardner, in the same roundtable, disputed his evidence and conclusions.

c-us7-viet-critics.text: In the H-Diplo roundtable Jessica Chapman, as Moyar quotes her, found 'fragmentary and often questionable use of evidence' and 'a disturbing lack of critical analysis throughout the book'; Lloyd Gardner, discussing an American invasion of North Vietnam, wrote that 'a more likely scenario would find the Americans without support among the populace.'
c-us7-viet-critics.label: debated
c-us7-viet-critics.note: The critics' words as quoted in Moyar's reply; their full reviews were not opened. Moyar replies that 'this dichotomy is not something I created.'

c-us7-68-king.text: King was shot 'At 6:05 P.M. on Thursday, 4 April 1968' at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, where he had come in support of 'striking Memphis sanitation workers.' News of his death 'prompted major outbreaks of racial violence, resulting in more than 40 deaths nationwide.' James Earl Ray pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 99 years.
c-us7-68-king.label: approx
c-us7-68-king.note: The death toll in the outbreaks is given only as 'more than 40'.

c-us7-68-rfk.text: On the night of 4 June 1968, the day of the California primary, Robert Kennedy declared victory to his supporters at the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles. 'Around 12:15 a.m.' on 5 June, 'just as he finished a speech and exited through the hotel kitchen', he was shot; he was pronounced dead at 1:44 a.m. on 6 June. Sirhan Sirhan 'was convicted of the murder of Kennedy.'
c-us7-68-rfk.label: consensus

c-us7-68-kerner.text: The Report of the National Advisory Commission on Civil Disorders (the Kerner Report, 1968) stated: 'This is our basic conclusion: Our nation is moving toward two societies, one black, one white—separate and unequal.' It also stated: 'White racism is essentially responsible for the explosive mixture which has been accumulating in our cities since the end of World War II.'
c-us7-68-kerner.label: consensus

c-us7-68-chicago.text: The Democratic National Convention in Chicago, 26-29 August 1968, nominated Hubert Humphrey. 'The largest clash between police and protesters occurred on August 28 in Grant Park', and the Walker Report found 'unrestrained and indiscriminate police violence.'
c-us7-68-chicago.label: consensus

c-us7-68-elec.text: In the 1968 presidential election Richard Nixon won 31,785,480 votes (43.4 percent) and 301 electoral votes; Hubert Humphrey 42.7 percent and 191 electoral votes; and George Wallace 13.5 percent and 46 electoral votes.
c-us7-68-elec.label: consensus

c-us7-68-delano.text: 'On September 8, 1965, hundreds of Filipino American farmworkers walked off' the vineyards of Delano, California, under Larry Itliong's Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee (AWOC). 'A week into the Delano Grape Strike, the NFWA joined.' The two later merged into the United Farm Workers, and the strike lasted five years.
c-us7-68-delano.label: consensus

c-us7-68-huerta.text: Dolores Huerta 'was the lead negotiator in getting the final contracts' in the Delano grape strike.
c-us7-68-huerta.label: consensus

c-us7-68-chicano.text: In March 1968 'approximately 15,000 high school students walked out' of schools in East Los Angeles. The Chicano Moratorium of 29 August 1970 drew '20,000 to 30,000 participants', and the journalist Rubén Salazar was killed that day by a deputy's tear-gas projectile.
c-us7-68-chicano.label: approx

c-us7-68-chavez.text: On 18 March 2026 NPR reported that 'a New York Times investigation out today reveals Chavez's alleged history of sexual assault'; NPR said it had not independently investigated the allegations, and Texas Public Radio said it 'has not independently verified any of the claims.' Dolores Huerta's statement, reported on 18 March, began: 'I am nearly 96 years old, and for the last 60 years have kept a secret because I believed that exposing the truth would hurt the farmworker movement I have spent my entire life fighting for.' The United Farm Workers said in a statement of 17 March that it had 'learned of deeply troubling allegations' that he 'behaved in ways that are incompatible with our organization's values', that 'Far more troubling are allegations involving abuse of young women or minors', and that it would not take part in Cesar Chavez Day activities on 31 March. The Cesar Chavez Foundation's statement, released the same day, said: 'We are deeply shocked and saddened by what we are hearing.' Chávez's family said in a statement reported on 18 March: 'Our family is devastated by today's New York Times article about our father, Cesar Chavez', and 'We wish peace and healing to the survivors and commend their courage to come forward'. In its obituary of Huerta on 28 October 2026 the Associated Press wrote that she had revealed that year 'that she was sexually abused in the 1960s by the farmworker movement's co-founder, César Chavez'.
c-us7-68-chavez.label: consensus

c-us7-68-huertadeath.text: On 28 October 2026 the Associated Press reported that Dolores Huerta had died at 96: 'Huerta's family said in a statement through her foundation that she died Wednesday at home.'
c-us7-68-huertadeath.label: consensus

c-us7-68-alcatraz.text: Indians of All Tribes occupied Alcatraz Island from 20 November 1969; the occupation 'lasted until June 11, 1971.' Afterwards, in the National Park Service's words, 'a policy of Indian self-determination became the official US government policy.'
c-us7-68-alcatraz.label: consensus

c-us7-68-wk.text: From 27 February 1973 about 200 Oglala Lakota and members of the American Indian Movement held the town of Wounded Knee, South Dakota, for 71 days, until 8 May. 'two protestors were shot and killed', and a U.S. Marshal was paralysed.
c-us7-68-wk.label: approx
c-us7-68-wk.note: The number of occupiers is an estimate.

c-us7-68-stonewall.text: 'In the early morning hours of June 28, 1969, a riot broke out in response to a police raid on the Stonewall Inn' in New York, with further demonstrations over the following days. The Stonewall National Monument was proclaimed on 24 June 2016.
c-us7-68-stonewall.label: consensus

c-us7-68-stonewallsite.text: On 14 February 2025 the Associated Press reported that 'the words "transgender" and "queer" had been deleted from text that had been on the site' of the Stonewall National Monument, and that 'The National Park Service did not respond to a message left Thursday seeking comment on the changes.' The monument's homepage, last updated on 9 July 2026, begins: 'Before the 1960s, almost everything about living authentically as a lesbian, a bisexual person or a gay man was illegal.'
c-us7-68-stonewallsite.label: consensus

c-us7-women-fm.text: Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique was 'published in 1963' and was 'an immediate best seller'. Britannica notes that Friedan called the discontent of American housewives 'the problem that has no name'.
c-us7-women-fm.label: consensus

c-us7-women-title7.text: On 8 February 1964 Representative Howard Smith, a Virginia Democrat, offered an amendment adding 'sex' to Title VII of the civil rights bill in the House; it carried 'by a teller vote of 168 to 133'.
c-us7-women-title7.label: consensus

c-us7-women-freeman.text: Jo Freeman (1991) argues that adding 'sex' to Title VII was 'not as thoughtless, or as devious, as has previously been assumed', and finds the pattern of the vote 'not consistent with' a plot to sink the bill.
c-us7-women-freeman.label: debated
c-us7-women-freeman.note: Freeman disputes the long-standing assumption, repeated in popular accounts, that Smith offered the amendment as a ploy to kill the bill; her case rests on the pattern of the vote.

c-us7-women-now.text: The National Organization for Women adopted its Statement of Purpose, written by Betty Friedan, on 29 October 1966: 'The purpose of NOW is to take action to bring women into full participation in the mainstream of American society now'.
c-us7-women-now.label: consensus

c-us7-women-era-senate.text: On 22 March 1972 the Senate passed the Equal Rights Amendment: '84 senators voted aye; eight, including Ervin, voted nay.' Its first section reads: 'Equality of rights under the law shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex.' Hawaii ratified it two hours later.
c-us7-women-era-senate.label: consensus

c-us7-women-era-states.text: Congress sent the ERA to the states 'with a seven-year deadline', later extended by three years, to 1982. 'By the end of the year, 22 states have ratified the Equal Rights Amendment' (1972); 'By 1977, only 35 states had ratified the ERA', and five of them, Nebraska, Tennessee, Idaho, Kentucky and South Dakota, voted to rescind.
c-us7-women-era-states.label: consensus

c-us7-women-era-later.text: Nevada ratified the ERA in 2017, 'the first state to ratify the measure since 1977'; 'In 2018, the Illinois legislature followed suit'; and 'On January 15, 2020, Virginia became the latest state to ratify'. With the five states that voted to rescind, that makes 38 ratifications, the three-quarters threshold.
c-us7-women-era-later.label: debated
c-us7-women-era-later.note: The count of 38 is this book's sum (35 plus three). Whether rescissions and ratifications after the deadline count is the legal dispute: the Brennan Center notes that Congress ignored purported rescissions when it declared the 14th and 15th Amendments ratified, and that a federal court in Idaho ruled in 1980 that Idaho's rescission was valid.

c-us7-women-title9.text: 'On June 23, 1972, President Richard M. Nixon signed the Education Amendments of 1972'. Title IX begins: 'No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in'.
c-us7-women-title9.label: consensus

c-us7-women-title9-sport.text: A resolution introduced in the Senate on 23 June 2022 and referred to committee (S.Res.692, 117th Congress) states that 'only 1 in 27 girls participated in school sports before title IX was enacted', against '2 in 5 girls now'.
c-us7-women-title9-sport.label: approx
c-us7-women-title9-sport.note: Figures stated in a resolution as introduced, not a statement adopted by the Senate, and not taken from a statistical agency.

c-us7-women-roe.text: Roe v. Wade was decided on 22 January 1973; 'MR. JUSTICE BLACKMUN delivered the opinion of the Court.'
c-us7-women-roe.label: consensus

c-us7-women-schlafly.text: In a 1972 issue of her newsletter Phyllis Schlafly announced her opposition to the ERA, and she then established STOP ERA; she founded the Eagle Forum in 1975. In Britannica's summary, she believed that women enjoyed 'unique privileges that the amendment would abolish' and contended that it 'would lead to military conscription for mothers'. Whether the ERA would have had these effects was the heart of the dispute with its supporters.
c-us7-women-schlafly.label: debated
c-us7-women-schlafly.note: Whether the ERA would have had these effects was the core of the dispute between Schlafly and ERA supporters such as NOW. Schlafly's views are given in Britannica's words, not her own.

c-us7-women-era-nara.text: On 17 December 2024 the Archivist of the United States, Colleen Shogan, and the Deputy Archivist stated that 'the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) cannot be certified as part of the Constitution', noting that 'In 2020 and again in 2022, the Office of Legal Counsel of the U.S. Department of Justice affirmed' the deadline and that court decisions 'at both the District and Circuit levels' had too; 'Therefore, the Archivist of the United States cannot legally publish the Equal Rights Amendment.'
c-us7-women-era-nara.label: consensus

c-us7-women-era-biden.text: In January 2025 President Biden declared of the ERA: 'It's the 28th amendment to the Constitution — now.' The White House said he would not order the Archivist to certify and publish it.
c-us7-women-era-biden.label: consensus

c-us7-women-era-courts.text: On 4 November 2025 the Ninth Circuit (Valame v. Trump) held that 'The ERA was not ratified by three-fourths of the States prior to the deadline set by Congress, June 30, 1982'; the plaintiff then 'received an extension to file a petition for a writ of certiorari', filed the petition on 9 March 2026, and on 22 June 2026 the Supreme Court denied it. On 21 April 2026 Judge William G. Young of the federal district court in Massachusetts 'rejected EQUAL MEANS EQUAL's argument concerning the ERA ratification deadline', and the group says it filed its opening brief in the First Circuit on 3 August 2026.
c-us7-women-era-courts.label: debated
c-us7-women-era-courts.note: A live dispute. Status as reported by the National Constitution Center (10 March 2026), the Supreme Court's docket (petition denied 22 June 2026) and Equal Means Equal, an advocacy group (6 August 2026). The Supreme Court's denial of review is not a ruling on the ERA's validity.

c-us7-women-era-debate.text: ERA supporters 'have long argued that just as Congress had the power to set a deadline, they have the power to lift one'; the Office of Legal Counsel (2020, 2022), the National Archives and the courts that have ruled so far hold the deadline binding. As of November 2026 the ERA has not been published as part of the Constitution.
c-us7-women-era-debate.label: debated
c-us7-women-era-debate.note: Supporters hold that Congress can lift its own deadline and that rescissions are invalid; the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel, the Archives and the courts so far hold that the 1982 deadline binds. The Supreme Court denied review in Valame on 22 June 2026 and has not ruled on the ERA's validity.

c-us7-women-lfp.text: Women's labor force participation rate, annual averages computed from FRED monthly data (BLS series LNU01300002, not seasonally adjusted): 33.9 percent in 1950, 37.7 in 1960, 43.4 in 1970, 46.4 in 1975 and 51.5 in 1980.
c-us7-women-lfp.label: approx
c-us7-women-lfp.note: Annual averages this book computed from the published monthly figures, rounded half up to one decimal; the BLS's own annual figures may differ slightly.

c-us7-nixon-china.text: Nixon 'travelled to Communist China February 21–28, 1972', 'becoming the first U.S. President to visit mainland China while in office'. In the Shanghai Communiqué the United States 'acknowledges that all Chinese on either side of the Taiwan Strait maintain that there is but one China'.
c-us7-nixon-china.label: consensus

c-us7-nixon-salt.text: In Moscow on 26 May 1972 Nixon and Brezhnev signed the ABM Treaty, which 'limited strategic missile defenses to 200 interceptors each and allowed each side to construct two missile defense sites', and the Interim Agreement of SALT I. The Office of the Historian writes that 'SALT I is considered the crowning achievement of the Nixon-Kissinger strategy of détente'.
c-us7-nixon-salt.label: consensus

c-us7-nixon-epa.text: The Environmental Protection Agency was set up under Reorganization Plan No. 3 of 9 July 1970, and 'on December 2, 1970, the Environmental Protection Agency would at last open its doors', with William Ruckelshaus as its first administrator.
c-us7-nixon-epa.label: consensus

c-us7-nixon-caa.text: The Clean Air Act of 1970 created national ambient air quality standards and 'resulted in a major shift in the federal government's role in air pollution control.'
c-us7-nixon-caa.label: consensus

c-us7-nixon-gold.text: On 15 August 1971 Nixon said: 'I have directed Secretary Connally to suspend temporarily the convertibility of the dollar into gold or other reserve assets'. He also announced 'a freeze on all prices and wages' for 90 days and 'an additional tax of 10 percent on goods imported'.
c-us7-nixon-gold.label: consensus

c-us7-nixon-float.text: The fixed-rate system did not survive. Under the Smithsonian Agreement of December 1971 the G-10 'agreed to a new set of fixed exchange rates centered on a devalued dollar', but in March 1973 'six members of the European Community tied their currencies together and jointly floated against the U.S. dollar', a decision that 'effectively signaled the abandonment of the Bretton Woods fixed exchange rate system.'
c-us7-nixon-float.label: consensus

c-us7-nixon-breakin.text: 'Early on the morning of June 17, 1972, five men broke into the Democratic National Committee headquarters.' The Senate created a select committee by unanimous vote on 7 February 1973, and its hearings were televised from May 1973.
c-us7-nixon-breakin.label: consensus

c-us7-nixon-tapes.text: Alexander Butterfield disclosed the White House taping system: 'on July 16, Butterfield repeated the disclosure in open committee testimony before live television cameras.'
c-us7-nixon-tapes.label: consensus

c-us7-nixon-massacre.text: In the 'Saturday Night Massacre' of 20 October 1973, Attorney General Elliot Richardson resigned, his deputy William Ruckelshaus was fired, and Robert Bork 'was ordered to fire special prosecutor Cox. He did.'
c-us7-nixon-massacre.label: consensus

c-us7-nixon-articles.text: The House Judiciary Committee 'adopted three articles of impeachment'; the first was 'adopted, 27 to 11'.
c-us7-nixon-articles.label: consensus

c-us7-nixon-usvnixon.text: United States v. Nixon was decided on 24 July 1974 by 8 votes to 0, with Justice Rehnquist not participating; Chief Justice Burger wrote: 'The generalized assertion of privilege must yield to the demonstrated, specific need for evidence in a pending criminal trial.' Neither the separation of powers nor the need for confidentiality, 'without more', could 'sustain an absolute, unqualified Presidential privilege of immunity from judicial process under all circumstances.'
c-us7-nixon-usvnixon.label: consensus

c-us7-nixon-resign.text: On 8 August 1974 Nixon told the nation: 'I shall resign the Presidency effective at noon tomorrow.'
c-us7-nixon-resign.label: consensus

c-us7-nixon-pardon.text: Gerald Ford's Proclamation 4311 of 8 September 1974 granted a 'full, free, and absolute pardon unto Richard Nixon for all offenses against the United States' for the period from 20 January 1969 to 9 August 1974.
c-us7-nixon-pardon.label: consensus

c-us7-70s-oil73.text: The oil embargo of the Organization of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries (OAPEC) began in October 1973. Its cuts 'nearly quadrupled the price of oil from $2.90 a barrel before the embargo to $11.65 a barrel in January 1974'; the embargo was lifted in March 1974.
c-us7-70s-oil73.label: consensus

c-us7-70s-oil79.text: In the second oil shock Iranian output fell '4.8 million barrels per day (7 percent of world production at the time) by January 1979', and oil prices were 'more than doubling between April 1979 and April 1980.'
c-us7-70s-oil79.label: consensus

c-us7-70s-oil79-cause.text: Graefe, writing in Federal Reserve History, says the loss of Iranian supply 'may not have been the most important factor' in the price rise: 'the Iranian disruption may have prompted a fear of further disruptions and spurred widespread speculative hoarding.'
c-us7-70s-oil79-cause.label: debated
c-us7-70s-oil79-cause.note: Graefe's assessment; the supply loss itself is not in dispute, only how much of the price rise it explains compared with fear of further disruptions and speculative hoarding.

c-us7-70s-carter.text: In his address to the nation of 15 July 1979 President Carter said: 'It is a crisis of confidence. It is a crisis that strikes at the very heart and soul and spirit of our national will.' He also said that 'too many of us now tend to worship self-indulgence and consumption.' The American Presidency Project titles the address 'The Malaise Speech'.
c-us7-70s-carter.label: consensus

c-us7-70s-campdavid.text: At the Camp David summit of 5-17 September 1978 Carter, Sadat and Begin produced 'two "Framework" documents', and Egypt and Israel signed a peace treaty in March 1979.
c-us7-70s-campdavid.label: consensus

c-us7-70s-airline.text: Signing the Airline Deregulation Act on 24 October 1978, Carter said: 'For the first time in decades, we have deregulated a major industry'; the act meant 'phasing out all activities of the Civil Aeronautics Board by 1985'.
c-us7-70s-airline.label: consensus

c-us7-70s-hostages.text: The American embassy in Tehran was seized on 4 November 1979; '52 United States citizens were held hostage for 444 days until January 20, 1981'. The rescue attempt, Operation Eagle Claw (24-25 April 1980), killed eight American servicemen.
c-us7-70s-hostages.label: consensus

c-us7-70s-volcker.text: On 6 October 1979 the Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker shifted 'to managing the volume of bank reserves'; the federal funds rate 'reached a record high of 20 percent in late 1980'.
c-us7-70s-volcker.label: consensus

c-us7-70s-peak.text: By the measure used in Federal Reserve History's essay, 'Inflation peaked at 11.6 percent in March' 1980; by the annual CPI-U measure, consumer prices rose 13.5 percent in 1980.
c-us7-70s-peak.label: approx
c-us7-70s-peak.note: Two different measures: a monthly peak in the essay, and the change in the annual average CPI-U.

c-us7-70s-cpi.label: approx
c-us7-70s-cpi.note: BLS CPI-U annual averages as published by the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, rounded to one decimal; other inflation measures give different figures.

c-us7-70s-unemp.text: Unemployment rate, annual averages computed from FRED monthly data (BLS series UNRATE, seasonally adjusted): 1969, 3.5 percent; 1970, 5.0; 1971, 6.0; 1972, 5.6; 1973, 4.9; 1974, 5.6; 1975, 8.5; 1976, 7.7; 1977, 7.1; 1978, 6.1; 1979, 5.9; 1980, 7.2; 1981, 7.6; 1982, 9.7.
c-us7-70s-unemp.label: approx
c-us7-70s-unemp.note: Annual averages this book computed from the monthly figures, rounded half up; the BLS's official annual averages can differ by 0.1 point.

c-us7-relig-engel.text: In Engel v. Vitale (25 June 1962), by 6 votes to 1, the Court struck down New York's Regents' prayer, which began 'Almighty God, we acknowledge our dependence upon Thee'. Justice Black wrote that 'it is no part of the business of government to compose official prayers'; Justice Stewart dissented.
c-us7-relig-engel.label: consensus

c-us7-relig-abington.text: In School District of Abington Township v. Schempp (17 June 1963), decided with Murray v. Curlett, the Court ruled 8-1, Justice Clark writing and Justice Stewart dissenting, against required Bible reading under the rule that 'At least ten verses from the Holy Bible shall be read, without comment'; Clark wrote that 'the Bible is worthy of study for its literary and historic qualities.'
c-us7-relig-abington.label: consensus

c-us7-relig-graham.text: Billy Graham's 1949 Los Angeles revival was extended 'to eight weeks'. In 1953 he 'Removes ropes separating blacks and whites at Chattanooga', and in 1957 he preached at Madison Square Garden 'for unprecedented 16 weeks; welcomes Martin Luther King Jr.', who prayed at the crusade on 18 July 1957. Britannica notes Graham's 'friendship with numerous U.S. presidents'.
c-us7-relig-graham.label: consensus

c-us7-relig-vatican2.text: The Second Vatican Council '(1962–65)' opened on 11 October 1962. Its constitution on the liturgy, Sacrosanctum Concilium (4 December 1963), allowed the use of the vernacular: 'the limits of its employment may be extended'.
c-us7-relig-vatican2.label: consensus

c-us7-relig-nostra.text: Nostra Aetate (28 October 1965) declared that what happened in Christ's passion 'cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today', and that 'the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God'.
c-us7-relig-nostra.label: consensus

c-us7-relig-jews67.text: During the week of the Six-Day War in June 1967 the United Jewish Appeal in the New York area 'raised more than $20 million', JTA reported in 2017.
c-us7-relig-jews67.label: approx

c-us7-relig-alterman.text: Eric Alterman writes in We Are Not One (2022): 'June 1967 transformed American Jews' relationship not only to Israel, but also to themselves.'
c-us7-relig-alterman.label: consensus

c-us7-relig-bobjones.text: Under a policy adopted in 1970 (Revenue Ruling 71-447), the IRS denied tax exemption to racially discriminatory private schools. In Bob Jones University v. United States (24 May 1983) the Court, 8-1, Chief Justice Burger writing and Justice Rehnquist dissenting, upheld its denial to a university whose rule was 'There is to be no interracial dating', holding that the government has 'a fundamental, overriding interest in eradicating racial discrimination in education'.
c-us7-relig-bobjones.label: consensus

c-us7-relig-mm.text: The Moral Majority, founded by Jerry Falwell in 1979, opposed 'abortion, pornography, the ERA, and gay rights', was 'credited with helping' elect Ronald Reagan in 1980, and dissolved in 1989.
c-us7-relig-mm.label: consensus

c-us7-relig-balmer.text: Randall Balmer argues that the religious right was set off by the fight over tax exemptions for segregated schools. He points to Green v. Connally, a ruling of the federal district court for the District of Columbia of 30 June 1971, which, as he quotes it, held that 'racially discriminatory private schools are not entitled to the Federal tax exemption', and writes: 'Green v. Connally served as the catalyst, not Roe v. Wade.' He quotes Paul Weyrich: 'It wasn't the abortion issue; that wasn't sufficient'.
c-us7-relig-balmer.label: debated

pages.title: Superpower and civil rights
pages.lede: In the Bureau of Economic Analysis's series real GDP roughly tripled between 1950 and 1980, while the population grew from about 140 million in 1945 to about 228 million in 1980. Real median family income rose about 74 percent from 1953 to 1973 and then changed little to 1980, and the official poverty rate fell from 22.4 percent in 1959 to 11.1 percent in 1973 before rising to 13.0 percent in 1980.
body: In the Bureau of Economic Analysis's series real GDP was $2,458.5 billion in 1950 and $7,257.3 billion in 1980, in chained 2017 dollars: it roughly tripled. The figure for 1945, $2,500.1 billion, is higher than that for 1950; on the wartime economy, see US6.0. [[c-us7-ov-gdp]] The population, also from BEA, rose from 139,928 thousand in 1945 to 227,726 thousand in 1980, from about 140 million to about 228 million. [[c-us7-ov-pop]] Dividing one series by the other, real GDP per person was about $16,200 in 1950 and about $31,900 in 1980: it roughly doubled, while the population grew by about half. [[c-us7-ov-percap]]

The Census Bureau's real median family income, measured in 2025 C-CPI-U dollars, was $41,880 in 1953, the series' first year, and $73,000 in 1973, a rise of about 74 percent. It was $69,850 in 1975 and $73,230 in 1980. [[c-us7-ov-income]] The official poverty rate was 22.4 percent in 1959, the first year measured, fell by about half to 11.1 percent in 1973, and was 13.0 percent in 1980. [[c-us7-ov-poverty]] Both series turned after 1973: income stopped rising and poverty rose. [[c-us7-ov-income]] [[c-us7-ov-poverty]] On the 1970s, see US7.12.

Each measure on this page comes from a single series, and each has its own units. The income series is now expressed in C-CPI-U dollars (R-CPI-U-RS before 2000), a changed deflator, so its levels differ from those in older printed tables, and it begins only in 1953; [[c-us7-ov-income]] chained-dollar GDP levels change with each BEA revision. [[c-us7-ov-gdp]] On the postwar world economy and Bretton Woods, see 15.13; on the Cold War worldwide, 15.9; on rights movements and religion worldwide, 15.14.

This chapter begins with containment (US7.1), the Red Scare (US7.2), Korea and the Eisenhower years (US7.3) and the postwar boom (US7.4). It then follows civil rights from 1945 to 1965 (US7.5-US7.6), Kennedy, Johnson and the Great Society (US7.7), Vietnam (US7.8), 1968 and the new movements (US7.9) and the women's movement (US7.10), and ends with Nixon (US7.11), the 1970s (US7.12) and religion and the rise of the religious right (US7.13). On the atomic bomb and the end of the war, see US6.13; on Brown v. Board and voting-rights doctrine, see US2.

pages.title: Containment
pages.lede: In February 1946 George Kennan's Long Telegram from Moscow described Soviet power as 'highly sensitive to logic of force'; in March 1947 the Truman Doctrine pledged to 'support free peoples', and the Marshall Plan's funding eventually rose to over $12 billion. The Berlin airlift, the North Atlantic Treaty of April 1949 and NSC-68 followed, while historians disagree about who began the Cold War.
body: On 22 February 1946 George Kennan, the American chargé d'affaires in the Soviet Union, sent the Secretary of State the message known as the Long Telegram. [[c-us7-cont-telegram]] He described Soviet power as 'a political force committed fanatically to the belief that with US there can be no permanent modus vivendi', and as 'Impervious to logic of reason, and it is highly sensitive to logic of force.' [[c-us7-cont-kennan]] His views also appeared in what the Office of the Historian calls 'an anonymous contribution to the journal Foreign Affairs, the so-called "X-Article."' [[c-us7-cont-x]] On the Cold War worldwide, see 15.9.

The Truman Doctrine of 12 March 1947 declared: 'I believe that it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures.' Truman requested $400,000,000 for Greece and Turkey. [[c-us7-cont-truman]] George Marshall announced the plan that bears his name in a speech to Harvard's graduating class on 5 June 1947, and Congress approved funding that would eventually rise to over $12 billion. [[c-us7-cont-marshall]]

The Berlin crisis, a Soviet blockade of West Berlin, began on 24 June 1948. In the American airlift that answered it, 'one plane landed every 45 seconds at Tempelhof Airport', and the blockade ended on 12 May 1949; the same Office of the Historian page also gives 11 May. [[c-us7-cont-berlin]] The North Atlantic Treaty was signed in Washington on 4 April 1949, and its members 'agreed to consider attack against one an attack against all.' [[c-us7-cont-nato]] NSC-68, 'completed by the U.S. Department of State's Policy Planning Staff on April 7, 1950', called for a massive build-up. After the Korean War began, defense spending 'almost tripled', from 5 to 14.2 percent of GDP between 1950 and 1953. [[c-us7-cont-nsc68]] On Korea, see US7.3.

Who began the Cold War? The orthodox historians, in Seth Center's summary, 'place primary responsibility for the Cold War on the Soviet Union'; many of them were 'former Roosevelt or Truman administration officials'. Center names Herbert Feis, among whose books is From Trust to Terror: The Onset of the Cold War, 1945-1950, and writes that these works 'emphasize Stalin's "ruthlessness," "spirit of mistrust," and revolutionary goals.' [[c-us7-cont-orthodox]] Revisionist historians, among them William Appleman Williams in The Tragedy of American Diplomacy (1959), argued, as Verso's online encyclopedia summarises them, that the United States had long had imperial ambitions. [[c-us7-cont-revisionist]] In 1983 John Lewis Gaddis described 'The Emerging Post-Revisionist Synthesis on the Origins of the Cold War'. Seth Center calls Gaddis that synthesis's 'first and foremost proponent' and writes that he 'concludes that the conflict grew out of external and internal conflict in both the Soviet Union and the United States.' [[c-us7-cont-gaddis]] For We Now Know (1997) Gaddis drew on newly opened Soviet archives. Reviewing it, Neal Ascherson described Gaddis as convinced that Stalin, more than anyone or anything else, brought about the Cold War, and wrote that the archives settled that Kim Il Sung had attacked South Korea first, in 1950. [[c-us7-cont-archives]]

pages.title: The Red Scare
pages.lede: A loyalty order of March 1947, the Hollywood Ten's contempt citations, Alger Hiss's conviction for perjury and the Rosenbergs' execution in June 1953 ran alongside Senator Joseph McCarthy's campaign, from his Wheeling speech of February 1950 to his censure by the Senate, 67 to 22, in December 1954. The Venona translations, made public from 1995, feed an argument between Haynes and Klehr, who stress Soviet espionage, and Ellen Schrecker, who stresses the harm of the anticommunist crusade.
body: Executive Order 9835, of 21 March 1947, provided: 'There shall be a loyalty investigation of every person entering the civilian employment of any department or agency' of the federal executive. [[c-us7-red-loyalty]] In October 1947 the Hollywood Ten refused to answer the questions of the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC), sitting in Washington. They were 'voted in contempt of Congress on November 24, 1947', received 'sentences of six months to one year in prison', and were blacklisted. [[c-us7-red-hollywood]] On the Red Scare after the First World War, see US5.13.

Whittaker Chambers accused Alger Hiss in 1948. On 21 January 1950 Hiss was found 'Guilty on two counts of perjury' and sentenced to five years. [[c-us7-red-hiss]] In what the FBI calls the atom spy case, 'On March 29, 1951, the jury rendered a verdict of guilty' against Julius and Ethel Rosenberg. Both were executed on 19 June 1953. [[c-us7-red-rosenberg]]

At Wheeling, West Virginia, on 9 February 1950, Senator Joseph McCarthy said, in the text printed by History Matters: 'I have here in my hand a list of 205 . . . a list of names that were made known to the Secretary of State'. The number is disputed: History Matters notes that advance copies of the speech given to the press 'record the number as 205', but that in a letter to Truman the next day and in the transcript McCarthy submitted to the Congressional Record ten days later 'he uses the number 57.' [[c-us7-red-wheeling]] The televised Army-McCarthy hearings, which began on 22 April 1954, 'showed McCarthy in an increasingly unattractive light', and on 2 December 1954 the Senate, 'on a vote of 67 to 22, censured Joseph McCarthy.' [[c-us7-red-censure]]

The United States 'began a secret program in February 1943 later codenamed VENONA' to break Soviet cables. It ran until 1980. The first of six public releases, in July 1995, 'included 49 messages', and over five more releases 'all of the approximately 3,000 VENONA translations were made public.' [[c-us7-red-venona]] The Department of Energy's history of the Manhattan Project names 'Julius Rosenberg, and Rosenberg's wife Ethel' among the spies Venona uncovered. [[c-us7-red-osti]] Ethel's own part is disputed. A memo of 22 August 1950 by the codebreaker Meredith Gardner, which the Associated Press described in 2024 as recently declassified, concluded that she knew of her husband's work 'but that due to illness she did not engage in the work herself'; the historian Harvey Klehr, as the AP reports, has written that she 'was an active participant in her husband's spy network.' [[c-us7-red-ethel]] Haynes and Klehr, authors of Venona and In Denial (2003), argue that Soviet espionage was extensive; their publisher's description says In Denial charges revisionist scholars with ignoring or distorting new evidence from Russian archives. [[c-us7-red-haynes]] The publisher's description of Ellen Schrecker's Many Are the Crimes (1998), reproduced by the National Humanities Center, calls it 'the first post-Cold War exploration of the anticommunist witch-hunt and its devastating impact'. Reviewing it, Alan Wald quotes her asking whether 'the espionage, which unquestionably occurred' required 'a politically repressive internal security system', and reports that her answer is no. [[c-us7-red-schrecker]]

pages.title: Korea and the Eisenhower years
pages.lede: The Department of Veterans Affairs counts 36,574 American deaths in the Korean theater, 33,739 of them in battle, and 17,672 more in service outside it; the National Park Service writes of 'over 50,000'. Truman relieved MacArthur in April 1951 and the armistice was signed on 27 July 1953; in 1956 Congress enlarged and funded the Interstate System, after Sputnik it passed the National Defense Education Act, and in 1961 Eisenhower warned against the 'military-industrial complex'.
body: How many Americans died in Korea? The Department of Veterans Affairs counts 33,739 battle deaths and 2,835 other deaths in theater: 36,574 in all. The National Park Service writes of 'over 50,000 American deaths'. The gap is mostly a matter of what is counted. The same VA fact sheet also lists 17,672 'Other Deaths in Service (Non-Theater)', and the three VA figures together come to 54,246. The historian Allan R. Millett explains that the Defense Department's older figures for 'other deaths' appear to have 'included all noncombat deaths throughout the armed forces, worldwide, during the entire Korean War era (1950–57)'. [[c-us7-kor-deaths]] On who attacked first, see US7.1; on the Cold War worldwide, 15.9.

'On April 11, 1951, President Truman officially relieved Douglas MacArthur of his command'; as the Truman Library puts Truman's reasoning, he felt the general had 'overstepped his authority, defied direct orders from his superior'. [[c-us7-kor-macarthur]] In 1952 Eisenhower pledged that 'he would personally go to Korea'. Armistice negotiations had gone on at Panmunjom for two years when, 'Finally, on July 27, 1953', the armistice was signed. [[c-us7-kor-armistice]]

The Federal-Aid Highway Act, signed on 29 June 1956, enlarged the Interstate System to 41,000 miles, from the 40,000 miles authorized in 1944, and paid for it. It 'authorizes $25 billion over the period 1957-1969 as the Federal share (90 percent)' and 'establishes the Highway Trust Fund.' The Senate's history of the act ties the roads to defense: 'transporting troops and for evacuating cities in case of nuclear attack'. [[c-us7-kor-highway]] Of Sputnik's launch on 4 October 1957 the Office of the Historian writes: 'The successful launch came as a shock to experts and citizens in the United States'. Congress answered with the National Defense Education Act, which 'made substantial funds available for low-cost student loans' and supported science, mathematics and foreign languages. [[c-us7-kor-sputnik]]

In his farewell address of 17 January 1961 Eisenhower said: 'In the councils of government, we must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence, whether sought or unsought, by the military-industrial complex. The potential for the disastrous rise of misplaced power exists and will persist.' He also warned that public policy 'could itself become the captive of a scientific-technological elite.' [[c-us7-kor-farewell]]
