pages.title: The postwar boom
pages.lede: By 1956, 7.8 million of 16 million Second World War veterans had taken part in education or training under the GI Bill, but scholars disagree about its racial effects, and Levittown, begun in 1947, barred Black families. About 76 million births came in the baby boom of 1946-1964, union membership peaked at about a third of workers, 'under God' entered the Pledge in 1954, and 'In God we trust' became the national motto in 1956.
body: The GI Bill was signed on 22 June 1944. By 1956 '7.8 million of 16 million World War II veterans had participated in an education or training program', and from 1944 to 1952 the Veterans Administration (today's Department of Veterans Affairs) backed nearly 2.4 million home loans. [[c-us7-boom-gibill]] On the postwar world economy, see 15.13.

Who gained? Publishers Weekly's review summarises Katznelson's argument in When Affirmative Action Was White (2005): the bill unfairly favoured white veterans by turning the administration of benefits over to local governments. [[c-us7-boom-katznelson]] Turner and Bound (2002) find 'a substantial and positive impact on the educational attainment of white men and black men born outside the South', but that 'for those black veterans likely to be limited to the South in their educational choices, the G.I. Bill had little effect on collegiate outcomes', widening the educational gap between Black and white men from southern states. [[c-us7-boom-turner]] The description of Mettler's Soldiers to Citizens by her literary agency presents the bill's benefits as reaching across lines of class and race. [[c-us7-boom-mettler]] Two new studies find widening racial gaps. Agbai, in a peer-reviewed article in the American Journal of Sociology (2025) on the bill's home-loan guaranty, finds that 'the GI Bill is linked with increased homeownership and home value for Black and White veterans', but that 'the policy exacerbated extant racial inequalities' in housing; Althoff and Szerman, in a working paper of June 2026 that has not yet been peer reviewed, estimate 'a 5-percentage-point (47 percent) widening of the racial college gap'. [[c-us7-boom-new]]

Levittown, on Long Island, begun in 1947, barred Black families. Its Clause 25 read: 'No dwelling shall be used or occupied by members of other than the Caucasian race'. It had 17,447 homes by November 1951, and in the Searchable Museum's words, 'Levittown refused to house Black veterans and their families.' [[c-us7-boom-levittown]] On civil rights, see US7.5. Pew Research Center counts 'a total of 76 million births during the boom' of 1946-1964, with annual births 'surpassing 4 million in 1954 and remaining above that level until 1965.' [[c-us7-boom-births]] Union membership peaked at about a third of workers: the Congressional Research Service cites 'a peak of 34.2% in 1945' in one series and 'its post-World War II peak of 33.5% in 1954' in another, against 10.1 percent of wage and salary workers in 2022 (9.4 percent on the measure behind the 1945 peak). [[c-us7-boom-unions]]

'Under God' entered the Pledge of Allegiance on 14 June 1954. Signing the bill, Eisenhower said that 'the millions of our school children will daily proclaim ... the dedication of our nation and our people to the Almighty.' [[c-us7-boom-pledge]] 'In God we trust' became the national motto under a law 'approved by the President on July 30, 1956', and was 'first used on paper money in 1957'. [[c-us7-boom-motto]] Gallup found church membership at 73 percent in 1937; it 'remained near 70% for the next six decades', and was 47 percent in 2020 (membership of a church, synagogue or mosque). [[c-us7-boom-church]] On religion and the rise of the religious right, see US7.13.

pages.title: Civil rights, 1945 to 1960
pages.sub: The armed forces, Till, Montgomery and Little Rock
pages.lede: In 1948 Truman ordered equal treatment in the armed services, and in 1956 southern members of Congress urged 'lawful means' of resistance to Brown v. Board of Education. Emmett Till was lynched in 1955, Montgomery's buses were boycotted for more than a year, and in 1957 Eisenhower sent paratroopers to Little Rock. Martin Luther King Jr. wrote that 'Christ furnished the spirit and motivation while Gandhi furnished the method.'
body: On 26 July 1948 President Truman issued Executive Order 9981, which declared 'equality of treatment and opportunity for all persons in the armed services'. In the National Archives' words, 'by the end of the Korean conflict, almost all of the military was integrated' (on Korea, see US7.3). [[c-us7-cr1-eo9981]] On 17 May 1954 the Supreme Court ruled in Brown v. Board of Education that segregated schools were 'inherently unequal'; for the case as doctrine, see US2.11. [[c-us7-cr1-littlerock]] On 12 March 1956 the Southern Manifesto, signed by 19 senators and 82 representatives, all from former Confederate states, was introduced in the House. It 'attacked Brown as an abuse of judicial power that trespassed upon states' rights' and urged southerners to exhaust all 'lawful means' of resistance. [[c-us7-cr1-manifesto]]

Emmett Till, a 14-year-old visiting relatives in Mississippi, was lynched on 28 August 1955. At the courthouse in Sumner an all-white, all-male jury acquitted Roy Bryant and J. W. Milam, who later confessed in a paid interview. [[c-us7-cr1-till]] His open-casket visitation and funeral were held at Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ in Chicago. On 25 July 2023 President Biden made that church, the Sumner courthouse and Graball Landing near Glendora, where Till's body is believed to have been recovered from the Tallahatchie River, into the Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley National Monument, which the Park Service calls America's 425th national park. [[c-us7-cr1-monument]] PBS NewsHour reports that Congress had failed to act against lynching 'more than 200 times' since 1900. The Emmett Till Antilynching Act, passed by the House 422 to 3, became law on 29 March 2022 and sets a maximum sentence of 30 years. [[c-us7-cr1-antilynch]]

In Montgomery, Rosa Parks was arrested on 1 December 1955. The bus boycott ran from 5 December 1955 to 20 December 1956, and the new Montgomery Improvement Association elected Martin Luther King Jr. its president. In Browder v. Gayle bus segregation was found unconstitutional, and the Supreme Court affirmed the ruling in November 1956. [[c-us7-cr1-boycott]] In September 1957 Governor Faubus called out the state's National Guard to surround Little Rock Central High School, and on 4 September nine Black students, known as the Little Rock Nine, attempted to enter. Eisenhower's Executive Order 10730 (the National Archives dates it 23 September; its transcript is signed 24 September) placed the Arkansas National Guard under federal control and sent 1,000 paratroopers of the 101st Airborne Division. [[c-us7-cr1-littlerock]]

The Southern Christian Leadership Conference, founded in January 1957 at Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta, 'drew on the power and independence of black churches' in its aim to redeem 'the soul of America.' [[c-us7-cr1-sclc]] King had studied personalism at Boston University under Brightman and DeWolf, a philosophy that, in the King Institute's words, 'emphasizes the necessity of personal religious experience in understanding God', and received his PhD in June 1955. [[c-us7-cr1-bu]] In 'Pilgrimage to Nonviolence' (1960) he wrote that Rauschenbusch's Christianity and the Social Crisis was a book that 'left an indelible imprint on my thinking', that 'Christ furnished the spirit and motivation while Gandhi furnished the method', and that Niebuhr 'made me aware of the complexity of human motives.' [[c-us7-cr1-king]] On rights movements and religion worldwide, see 15.14.

pages.title: Civil rights, 1960 to 1965
pages.sub: Sit-ins to the Voting Rights Act
pages.lede: The sit-ins of 1960, the Freedom Rides of 1961 and the Birmingham campaign of 1963, where King wrote that 'Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere', were followed by the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Black voter registration in Mississippi rose from 6.7 percent in 1965 to 74.2 percent in 1988.
body: On 1 February 1960 four students from North Carolina A&T sat in at the Woolworth's store in Greensboro. By the end of April 'over 50,000 students had participated', and the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) was founded on 15-17 April. [[c-us7-cr2-sitins]] The Freedom Riders left Washington on 4 May 1961. Near Anniston, Alabama, 'one of the buses was firebombed', and in Birmingham 'Bull' Connor's police 'offered no protection.' The Interstate Commerce Commission's ban on segregation took effect on 1 November 1961. [[c-us7-cr2-rides]]

The Birmingham campaign began on 3 April 1963, and King was arrested on Good Friday, 12 April. [[c-us7-cr2-bham]] In his Letter from Birmingham Jail, dated 16 April, he wrote: 'Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.' He wrote that 'This "Wait" has almost always meant "Never."' And he asked: 'Was not Amos an extremist for justice: "Let justice roll down like waters and righteousness like an ever flowing stream."' He went on to ask the same of Paul. [[c-us7-cr2-letter]] King's wording closely follows the Revised Standard Version: 'But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an everflowing stream.' The NRSVUE renders Amos 5:24 'But let justice roll down like water and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.' [[c-us7-cr2-amos]] On 3 May 'Commissioner Connor directed local police and fire departments to use force', and on 15 September Klansmen bombed the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church, 'killing four young girls.' [[c-us7-cr2-bham]]

On 28 August 1963 the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, with Bayard Rustin as march organiser, drew 'more than 200,000 demonstrators.' A. Philip Randolph had first called for a march on Washington in 1941, and on 26 March 1963 he telegraphed King that the Negro American Labor Council had begun planning a June march 'for Negro job rights'. [[c-us7-cr2-march]] The House passed the civil rights bill on 10 February 1964 by 290 to 130. [[c-us7-cr2-house]] Democrats voted 152 to 96 for it, Northern Democrats 141 to 4 and Southern Democrats 11 to 92; Republicans voted 138 to 34. [[c-us7-cr2-party]] The Senate debated the bill for sixty days. On 10 June it voted 71 to 29 for cloture, with 27 Republicans and 44 Democrats in the majority, and it passed the bill nine days later; Johnson signed it on 2 July 1964. [[c-us7-cr2-senate]] On the filibuster and cloture, see US2.3.

In the Freedom Summer of 1964 Michael Schwerner, James Chaney and Andrew Goodman disappeared in Mississippi on 21 June; their bodies were found on 4 August '14 feet below an earthen dam.' In 1967 seven men were convicted, 'none on murder charges', and Edgar Ray Killen was 'convicted of manslaughter on June 21, 2005.' [[c-us7-cr2-fs]] At the 1964 Democratic convention Fannie Lou Hamer of the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party told the credentials committee: 'If the Freedom Democratic Party is not seated now, I question America.' Offered a compromise of two at-large seats, Hamer replied: 'We didn't come all this way for no two seats.' [[c-us7-cr2-mfdp]] In Alabama, Jimmie Lee Jackson was shot on 18 February 1965, and 'Bloody Sunday' at the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma followed on 7 March. The march of 21-25 March swelled to 25,000 at Montgomery, and Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act on 6 August 1965. [[c-us7-cr2-selma]] Black registration rose: in Mississippi from 6.7 percent in March 1965 to 74.2 percent in November 1988, and in Alabama from 19.3 to 68.4 percent (chart). [[c-us7-cr2-reg]] For the Act in the courts, from Shelby County (2013) to Louisiana v. Callais (2026), see US2.5.

pages.title: Kennedy, Johnson and the Great Society
pages.lede: Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles from Cuba in October 1962, and Kennedy was killed in Dallas in November 1963. Johnson declared 'unconditional war on poverty' in January 1964 and in 1965 signed Medicare, Medicaid and an end to national-origins immigration quotas. The official poverty rate fell from 19.0 percent in 1964 to 11.1 percent in 1973; how much the programmes achieved is still argued over.
body: A U-2 flight on 14 October 1962 photographed missile sites in Cuba. Kennedy announced a 'quarantine' on 22 October, and on 28 October Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles. The United States pledged not to invade Cuba. Robert Kennedy told the Soviet ambassador, Anatoly Dobrynin, that the United States planned to remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey soon, but 'this could not be part of any public resolution of the missile crisis'; the Office of the Historian records that the missiles were removed in April 1963. [[c-us7-gs-cuba]] On the Cold War worldwide, see 15.9. Kennedy was killed in Dealey Plaza, Dallas, on 22 November 1963, and the Warren Commission concluded that 'Oswald acted alone.' [[c-us7-gs-jfk]] Under Executive Order 14176 the National Archives released 31,419 and then 37,127 pages of assassination records on 18 March 2025, smaller batches through 3 April 2025, and 11,022 more pages on 30 January 2026. [[c-us7-gs-files]]

In his State of the Union message of 8 January 1964 Johnson said: 'This administration today, here and now, declares unconditional war on poverty in America.' [[c-us7-gs-wop]] On 30 July 1965, at the Truman Library in Independence, Missouri, he signed the Social Security Amendments of 1965, which created Medicare and, under Title XIX, Medicaid; Harry and Bess Truman received the first Medicare insurance cards. [[c-us7-gs-medicare]] The Census Bureau's official poverty rate, which begins in 1959 at 22.4 percent, fell to 19.0 percent in 1964, 14.7 in 1966 and 11.1 in 1973 (chart). [[c-us7-gs-poverty]] For the aged it fell from 35.2 percent in 1959 to 16.3 percent in 1973. [[c-us7-gs-aged]]

On 3 October 1965, on Liberty Island, Johnson signed the immigration bill known as Hart-Celler. 'This bill that we will sign today is not a revolutionary bill,' he said, while condemning 'the harsh injustice of the national origins quota system'. The Act abolished that system and set caps of 120,000 for the Western Hemisphere and 170,000 for the rest of the world. [[c-us7-gs-hc]] Pew Research Center (2015) estimates that 'roughly 59 million immigrants' arrived from 1965 to 2015, that the foreign-born share rose 'from 5% in 1965 to 14%', and that of these immigrants 'half (51%) are from Latin America and one-quarter are from Asia.' [[c-us7-gs-pew]]

Did the programmes work? Charles Murray's Losing Ground (1984), as the Manhattan Institute describes it, argues that the social programmes of the 1960s and 1970s made matters worse for their supposed beneficiaries, the poor and minorities. [[c-us7-gs-murray]] The contributors to Legacies of the War on Poverty (2013), edited by Martha J. Bailey and Sheldon Danziger, judge that popular view too negative, as their publisher summarises the book. [[c-us7-gs-legacies]] Christopher Wimer and his co-authors (2016), using an anchored Supplemental Poverty Measure, find that from 1967 to 2012 'poverty rates have dropped by 40 %' and that 'government policies, not market incomes, are driving the declines.' [[c-us7-gs-wimer]] Richard Burkhauser and his co-authors, using an absolute full-income measure, report that 'our absolute FPM rate fell from 19.5 to 1.6 percent' from 1963 to 2019, but that relative poverty fell only 'from 19.5 to 16.0 percent'. [[c-us7-gs-burk]]

pages.title: Vietnam
pages.lede: In August 1964 Congress approved the president's determination 'to take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack' against American forces. American troops in Vietnam numbered 537,000 at the end of 1968, the year 16,899 Americans died there, before Saigon fell on 30 April 1975. At home came the draft lottery, the Moratorium and the shootings at Kent State and Jackson State; historians still divide over whether the war was necessary and winnable.
body: The Tonkin Gulf Resolution, passed on 7 August 1964, approved the president's determination 'to take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack against the forces of the United States'. [[c-us7-viet-tonkin]] The Senate passed it 88 to 2, with Senators Morse and Gruening against. The House vote is recorded as 416 to 0 in the State Department's documentary history, Foreign Relations of the United States, and in the Voteview roll-call record, as James M. Lindsay of the Council on Foreign Relations also gives it; Britannica and the Defense Department's Vietnam War commemoration give 414 to 0. [[c-us7-viet-votes]] A National Security Agency report of 2002, made available in 2007, confirmed an attack on 2 August but 'concluded the August 4 attack never happened.' The resolution was repealed in January 1971, in the National Archives' words 'in an attempt to curtail President Nixon's power to continue the war.' [[c-us7-viet-tonkin]] On war powers and the War Powers Resolution, see US2.12.

By Edwin Moïse's tabulation, American military personnel in Vietnam numbered 23,300 at the end of 1964, 184,000 at the end of 1965 and 537,000 at the end of 1968, and 539,000 at mid-1969, falling to 24,000 at the end of 1972 (chart). [[c-us7-viet-troops]] The National Archives lists 58,220 American military fatal casualties, 47,434 from hostile and 10,786 from non-hostile causes; the highest yearly toll was 16,899, in 1968. [[c-us7-viet-deaths]] The Tet offensive began on 30 January 1968, when about 84,000 troops attacked 36 provincial capitals and 64 district towns. In the Defense Department commemoration's words, 'The offensive shocks the American public.' [[c-us7-viet-tet]]

At home, 'A lottery drawing – the first since 1942 – was held on December 1, 1969' for men born from 1944 to 1950; the first date drawn was 14 September. The last draft call came on 7 December 1972, and the authority to induct ended on 30 June 1973. [[c-us7-viet-draft]] On 15 October 1969 'Over two million people across the United States' joined the Moratorium to End the War in Vietnam. [[c-us7-viet-mora]] At Kent State University on 4 May 1970 the Ohio National Guard fired 'between 61 and 67 shots' in 'a 13-second period', 'killing four and wounding nine.' [[c-us7-viet-kent]] At Jackson State on 14-15 May, city police and highway patrolmen fired 'nearly 400 rounds of bullets and buckshot over 28 seconds in every direction', and they 'turned on Alexander Hall, a women's dormitory.' Phillip Gibbs and James Green were killed, and 'Twelve people were shot by the police and survived.' [[c-us7-viet-jackson]] In June 1971 the Pentagon Papers, a study of about 7,000 pages commissioned by McNamara in 1967, were leaked. In New York Times Co. v. United States, on 30 June, the Court stated that 'Any system of prior restraints of expression comes to this Court bearing a heavy presumption against its constitutional validity.' The full report was released in 2011. [[c-us7-viet-pp]] On the press clause, see US2.9.

The peace agreement was signed on 27 January 1973. On 29 April 1975 Operation Frequent Wind took 'over 7,000 personnel—primarily Americans and Vietnamese' out of Saigon, and the next day 'NVA tanks rolled through the gate of the Presidential Palace in Saigon, effectively ending the war.' [[c-us7-viet-saigon]] The historian Michael G. Kort, who himself argues that the war 'could and should have been won at far less cost than the United States, South Vietnam, and their allies suffered in defeat', frames the debate as two questions: was the war necessary and wise, and, once the United States was involved, 'was that war winnable?' The orthodox narrative, whose proponents he says include the journalists David Halberstam, Frances FitzGerald, Stanley Karnow and Neil Sheehan, and which he says 'also became the prevailing viewpoint among American academics', 'answers both questions firmly in the negative'; the revisionist narrative answers both in the affirmative, holding that the United States went to war 'without first developing a strategy for victory'. [[c-us7-viet-kort]] Against the revisionists, Fredrik Logevall, author of Choosing War (1999), said: 'The Vietnam tragedy, which we are still living with in so many ways, which led to deaths of millions, was an unnecessary war'. [[c-us7-viet-logevall]] Mark Moyar's Triumph Forsaken (2006), which James McAllister, as Moyar quotes him, said 'can rightfully claim to be the most consequential revisionist book ever produced on the Vietnam War', shows, in Moyar's own description, 'how Diem consolidated control over a badly fractured country' and 'how the removal of Diem crippled South Vietnam's ability to fight the Communists.' [[c-us7-viet-moyar]] Critics answered in the same H-Diplo roundtable: Jessica Chapman, as Moyar quotes her, found 'a disturbing lack of critical analysis throughout the book', and Lloyd Gardner, discussing an American invasion of North Vietnam, wrote that 'a more likely scenario would find the Americans without support among the populace.' [[c-us7-viet-critics]]

pages.title: 1968 and new movements
pages.lede: In 1968 King and Robert Kennedy were shot, the Kerner Report concluded that the nation was 'moving toward two societies', police and protesters clashed during the Democratic convention in Chicago, and Nixon won the presidency with 43.4 percent of the vote. Farmworkers struck in Delano, Chicano students walked out in Los Angeles, American Indian activists held Alcatraz and Wounded Knee, and a riot followed a police raid on the Stonewall Inn.
body: King was shot 'At 6:05 P.M. on Thursday, 4 April 1968' at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, where he had come in support of 'striking Memphis sanitation workers.' News of his death 'prompted major outbreaks of racial violence, resulting in more than 40 deaths nationwide.' James Earl Ray pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 99 years. [[c-us7-68-king]] On the night of 4 June, the day of the California primary, Robert Kennedy declared victory to his supporters at the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles. Around 12:15 a.m. on 5 June, as he left through the hotel kitchen, he was shot; he was pronounced dead at 1:44 a.m. on 6 June, and Sirhan Sirhan was convicted of his murder. [[c-us7-68-rfk]]

The Report of the National Advisory Commission on Civil Disorders, the Kerner Report, stated in 1968: 'This is our basic conclusion: Our nation is moving toward two societies, one black, one white—separate and unequal.' It also stated: 'White racism is essentially responsible for the explosive mixture which has been accumulating in our cities since the end of World War II.' [[c-us7-68-kerner]] The Democratic convention in Chicago, 26-29 August, nominated Hubert Humphrey. 'The largest clash between police and protesters occurred on August 28 in Grant Park', and the Walker Report found 'unrestrained and indiscriminate police violence.' [[c-us7-68-chicago]] Richard Nixon won 43.4 percent of the popular vote and 301 electoral votes, Humphrey 42.7 percent and 191, and George Wallace 13.5 percent and 46. [[c-us7-68-elec]]

'On September 8, 1965, hundreds of Filipino American farmworkers walked off' the vineyards of Delano, California, under Larry Itliong's Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee; 'A week into the Delano Grape Strike, the NFWA joined.' The two later merged into the United Farm Workers, and the strike lasted five years. [[c-us7-68-delano]] Dolores Huerta 'was the lead negotiator in getting the final contracts.' [[c-us7-68-huerta]] In March 1968 'approximately 15,000 high school students walked out' of schools in East Los Angeles, and the Chicano Moratorium of 29 August 1970 drew '20,000 to 30,000 participants'; that day the journalist Rubén Salazar was killed by a deputy's tear-gas projectile. [[c-us7-68-chicano]] On 18 March 2026 NPR reported that 'a New York Times investigation out today reveals Chavez's alleged history of sexual assault'; NPR said it had not independently investigated the allegations, and Texas Public Radio that it 'has not independently verified any of the claims.' Huerta's statement, reported on 18 March, began: 'I am nearly 96 years old, and for the last 60 years have kept a secret because I believed that exposing the truth would hurt the farmworker movement I have spent my entire life fighting for.' The United Farm Workers said in a statement of 17 March that it had 'learned of deeply troubling allegations' that Chávez 'behaved in ways that are incompatible with our organization's values', and that it would not take part in Cesar Chavez Day activities on 31 March. The Cesar Chavez Foundation said the same day: 'We are deeply shocked and saddened by what we are hearing.' Chávez's family said: 'Our family is devastated by today's New York Times article about our father, Cesar Chavez', and 'We wish peace and healing to the survivors and commend their courage to come forward'. [[c-us7-68-chavez]] In its obituary of Huerta on 28 October 2026, the Associated Press wrote that she had revealed that year that she was sexually abused in the 1960s by César Chávez, the farmworker movement's co-founder, and reported that she had died at home at 96. [[c-us7-68-chavez]] [[c-us7-68-huertadeath]]

Indians of All Tribes occupied Alcatraz Island from 20 November 1969 until 11 June 1971. Afterwards, in the National Park Service's words, 'a policy of Indian self-determination became the official US government policy.' [[c-us7-68-alcatraz]] On 27 February 1973 about 200 Oglala Lakota and members of the American Indian Movement took Wounded Knee, South Dakota, and held it for 71 days, until 8 May; 'two protestors were shot and killed', and a U.S. Marshal was paralysed. [[c-us7-68-wk]] In New York, 'In the early morning hours of June 28, 1969, a riot broke out in response to a police raid on the Stonewall Inn', and demonstrations followed over the next days; the Stonewall National Monument was proclaimed on 24 June 2016. [[c-us7-68-stonewall]] On 14 February 2025 the Associated Press reported that the words 'transgender' and 'queer' had been deleted from the monument's National Park Service website, and that the Park Service had not responded to a request for comment. The homepage, last updated on 9 July 2026, begins: 'Before the 1960s, almost everything about living authentically as a lesbian, a bisexual person or a gay man was illegal.' [[c-us7-68-stonewallsite]] On the women's movement, see US7.10.

pages.title: The women's movement
pages.lede: Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963) wrote of 'the problem that has no name'; in 1964 the House added 'sex' to Title VII, and in 1966 NOW set out to bring women into 'full participation' in American life. In 1972 the Senate passed the Equal Rights Amendment and Nixon signed Title IX, while women's labor force participation rose from about 34 percent in 1950 to about 51 percent in 1980. Phyllis Schlafly's STOP ERA fought ratification, and as of November 2026 the amendment has not been published as part of the Constitution.
body: Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique was published in 1963 and became an immediate best seller; Britannica notes that Friedan called the discontent of American housewives 'the problem that has no name'. [[c-us7-women-fm]] On 8 February 1964 Representative Howard Smith, a Virginia Democrat, offered an amendment in the House adding 'sex' to Title VII of the civil rights bill, and it carried by a teller vote of 168 to 133. [[c-us7-women-title7]] (On the Civil Rights Act as a whole, see US7.6.) It has often been assumed that Smith meant to sink the bill. Jo Freeman (1991) argues that the addition was 'not as thoughtless, or as devious, as has previously been assumed', and finds the pattern of the vote 'not consistent with' a plot to kill the bill. [[c-us7-women-freeman]]

On 29 October 1966 the National Organization for Women adopted a Statement of Purpose written by Friedan: 'The purpose of NOW is to take action to bring women into full participation in the mainstream of American society now'. [[c-us7-women-now]] On 22 March 1972 the Senate passed the Equal Rights Amendment: '84 senators voted aye; eight, including Ervin, voted nay.' Its first section reads: 'Equality of rights under the law shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex.' Hawaii ratified it two hours later. [[c-us7-women-era-senate]] On 23 June 1972 Nixon signed the Education Amendments of 1972, whose Title IX begins: 'No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in'. [[c-us7-women-title9]] A resolution introduced in the Senate in June 2022 states that only 1 in 27 girls took part in school sports before Title IX, against 2 in 5 when it was written. [[c-us7-women-title9-sport]] On 22 January 1973 the Court decided Roe v. Wade, Justice Blackmun writing; for the doctrine and Dobbs, see US2.11. [[c-us7-women-roe]]

Congress sent the ERA to the states with a seven-year deadline, later extended to 1982. By the end of 1972, 22 states had ratified, and by 1977, 35; five of them, Nebraska, Tennessee, Idaho, Kentucky and South Dakota, voted to rescind their ratifications. [[c-us7-women-era-states]] In 1972 Phyllis Schlafly announced her opposition to the ERA and then founded STOP ERA; she founded the Eagle Forum in 1975. In Britannica's summary, she believed that women enjoyed 'unique privileges that the amendment would abolish' and contended that it 'would lead to military conscription for mothers'; whether the amendment would have had those effects was the heart of the dispute with its supporters. [[c-us7-women-schlafly]] Meanwhile women's labor force participation, averaged from monthly BLS data, rose from about 34 percent in 1950 to about 43 percent in 1970 and about 51 percent in 1980. [[c-us7-women-lfp]]

Nevada ratified in 2017, the first state to do so since 1977; Illinois followed in 2018 and Virginia on 15 January 2020. With the five states that voted to rescind, that makes 38, the three-quarters threshold, and whether rescissions and ratifications after the deadline count is the legal question. [[c-us7-women-era-later]] On 17 December 2024 the Archivist, Colleen Shogan, and her deputy stated that the ERA 'cannot be certified as part of the Constitution', citing the Office of Legal Counsel's opinions of 2020 and 2022 and court decisions, and concluded that 'the Archivist of the United States cannot legally publish the Equal Rights Amendment.' [[c-us7-women-era-nara]] In January 2025 President Biden declared it 'the 28th amendment to the Constitution', but the White House said he would not order the Archivist to certify and publish it. [[c-us7-women-era-biden]] On 4 November 2025 the Ninth Circuit held, in Valame v. Trump, that 'The ERA was not ratified by three-fourths of the States prior to the deadline set by Congress, June 30, 1982'; the plaintiff petitioned the Supreme Court on 9 March 2026. On 21 April 2026 Judge William G. Young in Massachusetts rejected Equal Means Equal's argument about the deadline. On 22 June 2026 the Supreme Court denied review in Valame. On 3 August 2026, by its own account, Equal Means Equal filed its opening brief in the First Circuit. [[c-us7-women-era-courts]] Supporters argue, in the Brennan Center's words, that 'just as Congress had the power to set a deadline, they have the power to lift one'; the Office of Legal Counsel, the Archives and the courts so far hold the deadline binding. As of November 2026 the ERA has not been published as part of the Constitution (see US2.8). [[c-us7-women-era-debate]]

pages.title: Nixon
pages.sub: Détente, the dollar and Watergate, 1969 to 1974
pages.lede: In 1972 Nixon became the first president to visit mainland China while in office and signed the ABM Treaty and SALT I in Moscow; at home the EPA opened in 1970, and in August 1971 he suspended the dollar's convertibility into gold. The Watergate break-in of June 1972 led to Senate hearings, the public disclosure of the White House taping system and, on 24 July 1974, an 8-0 ruling that a generalized claim of privilege must yield to the needs of a criminal trial. Nixon announced his resignation on 8 August 1974, and a month later Ford pardoned him.
body: Nixon travelled to China from 21 to 28 February 1972, the first American president to visit mainland China while in office. In the Shanghai Communiqué the United States 'acknowledges that all Chinese on either side of the Taiwan Strait maintain that there is but one China'. [[c-us7-nixon-china]] In Moscow on 26 May 1972 he and Brezhnev signed the ABM Treaty, which 'limited strategic missile defenses to 200 interceptors each and allowed each side to construct two missile defense sites', together with the Interim Agreement of SALT I. The State Department's historians write that SALT I 'is considered the crowning achievement of the Nixon-Kissinger strategy of détente'. [[c-us7-nixon-salt]] For the Cold War as a whole, see 15.9.

The Environmental Protection Agency, set up under Reorganization Plan No. 3 of 9 July 1970, opened its doors on 2 December 1970, with William Ruckelshaus as its first administrator. [[c-us7-nixon-epa]] The Clean Air Act of 1970 created national ambient air quality standards and, in the EPA's words, 'resulted in a major shift in the federal government's role in air pollution control.' [[c-us7-nixon-caa]] On 15 August 1971 Nixon told the nation: 'I have directed Secretary Connally to suspend temporarily the convertibility of the dollar into gold or other reserve assets'. He also announced 'a freeze on all prices and wages' for 90 days and 'an additional tax of 10 percent on goods imported'. [[c-us7-nixon-gold]] The fixed-rate system did not survive. The Smithsonian Agreement of December 1971 set 'a new set of fixed exchange rates centered on a devalued dollar', but in March 1973 six European Community currencies began a joint float against the dollar, which, in the Office of the Historian's words, 'effectively signaled the abandonment of the Bretton Woods fixed exchange rate system.' On Bretton Woods, see 15.13. [[c-us7-nixon-float]]

Watergate began 'Early on the morning of June 17, 1972,' when 'five men broke into the Democratic National Committee headquarters.' The Senate voted unanimously on 7 February 1973 to create a select committee, whose hearings were televised from May 1973. [[c-us7-nixon-breakin]] On 16 July 1973 Alexander Butterfield made the White House taping system public: he 'repeated the disclosure in open committee testimony before live television cameras.' [[c-us7-nixon-tapes]] On 20 October 1973, in the 'Saturday Night Massacre', Attorney General Elliot Richardson resigned and his deputy William Ruckelshaus was fired; Robert Bork then 'was ordered to fire special prosecutor Cox. He did.' [[c-us7-nixon-massacre]] The House Judiciary Committee adopted three articles of impeachment, the first by 27 votes to 11. [[c-us7-nixon-articles]]

On 24 July 1974, in United States v. Nixon, the Supreme Court ruled 8-0, with Justice Rehnquist not taking part. Chief Justice Burger wrote: 'The generalized assertion of privilege must yield to the demonstrated, specific need for evidence in a pending criminal trial.' Neither the separation of powers nor the need for confidentiality, 'without more', he held, could 'sustain an absolute, unqualified Presidential privilege of immunity from judicial process under all circumstances.' [[c-us7-nixon-usvnixon]] (On presidential immunity and impeachment as doctrine, see US2.4.) On 8 August 1974 Nixon told the nation: 'I shall resign the Presidency effective at noon tomorrow.' [[c-us7-nixon-resign]] On 8 September President Ford's Proclamation 4311 granted a 'full, free, and absolute pardon unto Richard Nixon for all offenses against the United States' for the period from 20 January 1969 to 9 August 1974. [[c-us7-nixon-pardon]]

pages.title: The 1970s
pages.lede: The oil embargo of 1973-74 nearly quadrupled the price of oil, and after Iranian output fell, prices more than doubled between April 1979 and April 1980; consumer prices rose 11.1 percent in 1974 and 13.5 percent in 1980, while unemployment averaged about 8.5 percent in 1975. Carter, Sadat and Begin produced the Camp David frameworks in 1978, Carter signed airline deregulation, and in July 1979 he spoke of 'a crisis of confidence'. That autumn the Federal Reserve under Volcker turned to managing bank reserves, and the embassy in Tehran was seized, its 52 American hostages held for 444 days.
body: The oil embargo of the Organization of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries (OAPEC) began in October 1973. Its cuts 'nearly quadrupled the price of oil from $2.90 a barrel before the embargo to $11.65 a barrel in January 1974', and the embargo was lifted in March 1974. [[c-us7-70s-oil73]] In the second shock Iranian output fell by '4.8 million barrels per day (7 percent of world production at the time) by January 1979', and oil prices were 'more than doubling between April 1979 and April 1980.' [[c-us7-70s-oil79]] Graefe, writing in Federal Reserve History, says the loss of supply 'may not have been the most important factor', pointing instead to 'a fear of further disruptions' and 'widespread speculative hoarding'. [[c-us7-70s-oil79-cause]] On oil and the world economy, see 15.13.

Consumer prices (CPI-U) rose 5.5 percent in 1969, 11.1 percent in 1974, 9.1 percent in 1975 and 13.5 percent in 1980; they rose in every year from 1969 to 1982. [[c-us7-70s-cpi]] Unemployment, averaged from the monthly BLS figures, went from about 3.5 percent in 1969 and 4.9 percent in 1973 to about 8.5 percent in 1975 and 9.7 percent in 1982. [[c-us7-70s-unemp]] In 1975, then, prices rose 9.1 percent while unemployment averaged about 8.5 percent. [[c-us7-70s-cpi]] [[c-us7-70s-unemp]]

At Camp David from 5 to 17 September 1978, Carter, Sadat and Begin produced 'two "Framework" documents', and Egypt and Israel signed a peace treaty in March 1979. [[c-us7-70s-campdavid]] Signing the Airline Deregulation Act on 24 October 1978, Carter said: 'For the first time in decades, we have deregulated a major industry'; the act meant 'phasing out all activities of the Civil Aeronautics Board by 1985'. [[c-us7-70s-airline]] In his address to the nation of 15 July 1979 he said: 'It is a crisis of confidence. It is a crisis that strikes at the very heart and soul and spirit of our national will.' He also said that 'too many of us now tend to worship self-indulgence and consumption.' The American Presidency Project titles it 'The Malaise Speech'. [[c-us7-70s-carter]]

On 6 October 1979 the Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker shifted 'to managing the volume of bank reserves', and the federal funds rate 'reached a record high of 20 percent in late 1980'. [[c-us7-70s-volcker]] By the measure the Federal Reserve History essay uses, 'Inflation peaked at 11.6 percent in March' 1980; by the annual CPI-U measure, prices rose 13.5 percent that year. [[c-us7-70s-peak]] On 4 November 1979 the American embassy in Tehran was seized, and '52 United States citizens were held hostage for 444 days until January 20, 1981'. A rescue attempt, Operation Eagle Claw, on 24-25 April 1980, killed eight American servicemen. [[c-us7-70s-hostages]]

pages.title: Religion and the rise of the religious right
pages.lede: In 1957 Billy Graham preached for 16 weeks at Madison Square Garden. In 1962 and 1963 the Supreme Court struck down an official school prayer and required Bible reading, while Vatican II allowed the vernacular in the liturgy, and in 1965 Nostra Aetate declared that what happened in Christ's passion cannot be charged against all the Jews. In the week of the Six-Day War of 1967 the New York-area United Jewish Appeal raised more than $20 million, and in 1983 the Court upheld the IRS's denial of tax exemption to Bob Jones University. Historians disagree about what launched the religious right, whose Moral Majority Jerry Falwell founded in 1979: Randall Balmer points to the fight over segregated schools, Daniel K. Williams to issues of gender, sexuality and nationalism.
body: On 25 June 1962, in Engel v. Vitale, the Supreme Court struck down, by 6 votes to 1, New York's Regents' prayer, which began 'Almighty God, we acknowledge our dependence upon Thee'. Justice Black wrote that 'it is no part of the business of government to compose official prayers'. [[c-us7-relig-engel]] On 17 June 1963, in School District of Abington Township v. Schempp, decided with Murray v. Curlett, the Court ruled 8-1 against required Bible reading under the rule that 'At least ten verses from the Holy Bible shall be read, without comment'. Yet Justice Clark wrote that 'the Bible is worthy of study for its literary and historic qualities.' Justice Stewart dissented in both cases. [[c-us7-relig-abington]] For the doctrine, see US2.9.

Billy Graham's 1949 revival in Los Angeles was extended to eight weeks. In 1953 at Chattanooga he removed the ropes separating Black and white listeners, and in 1957 he preached at Madison Square Garden for 16 weeks and welcomed Martin Luther King Jr., who prayed at the crusade on 18 July 1957. Britannica notes Graham's friendship with numerous presidents. [[c-us7-relig-graham]] The Second Vatican Council (1962-65) allowed the vernacular in the liturgy: in Sacrosanctum Concilium (4 December 1963) it ruled that 'the limits of its employment may be extended'. [[c-us7-relig-vatican2]] Its declaration Nostra Aetate (28 October 1965) taught that what happened in Christ's passion 'cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today', and that 'the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God'. [[c-us7-relig-nostra]]

In the week of the Six-Day War in June 1967, the United Jewish Appeal in the New York area raised more than $20 million, JTA reported. [[c-us7-relig-jews67]] Eric Alterman writes that 'June 1967 transformed American Jews' relationship not only to Israel, but also to themselves.' [[c-us7-relig-alterman]] From 1970 the IRS denied tax exemption to racially discriminatory private schools. In Bob Jones University v. United States (24 May 1983) the Court, 8-1, upheld its denial to a university whose rule was 'There is to be no interracial dating', holding that the government has 'a fundamental, overriding interest in eradicating racial discrimination in education'. [[c-us7-relig-bobjones]] Jerry Falwell founded the Moral Majority in 1979. It opposed 'abortion, pornography, the ERA, and gay rights', was 'credited with helping' elect Ronald Reagan in 1980, and dissolved in 1989. [[c-us7-relig-mm]]

What set off the religious right is debated. Randall Balmer points to Green v. Connally, a ruling of the federal district court for the District of Columbia of 30 June 1971, which, as he quotes it, held that 'racially discriminatory private schools are not entitled to the Federal tax exemption'. 'Green v. Connally served as the catalyst, not Roe v. Wade,' he writes, and he quotes Paul Weyrich: 'It wasn't the abortion issue; that wasn't sufficient'. [[c-us7-relig-balmer]] Daniel K. Williams holds instead that the IRS issue 'was simply one factor among many in the formation of a conservative Republican evangelical coalition', and that 'issues of gender, sexuality, and nationalism played a much greater role than race in the mobilization of Christian conservatives.' [[c-us7-relig-williams]] In a 2015 article he traces the pro-life movement to Catholic founders of the late 1960s, many of them liberal Democrats, and argues that evangelicals who joined in the late 1970s recast it as a conservative cause. [[c-us7-relig-williams-prolife]] Roe v. Wade itself was decided on 22 January 1973 (see US7.10). [[c-us7-women-roe]]
